subsubtopic: GOVERNMENT'S INTENTION WITH REGARD TO IMPLEMENTATION OF MARIN REPORT-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, relating to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Since the Marin Commission Report on internal discipline and other aspects of the RCMP procedures has been in the hands of the government since January 1976, and since the need for its implementation is clearly illustrated in an incident such as L'Agence de Presse Libre burglary which involved an RCMP officer assigned to the investigation of this burglary for which he had some responsibility, as pointed out on page 15007 of Hansard last July, who was disciplined by the RCMP, then promoted by the RCMP, and finally it became necessary for him to enter a guilty plea respecting the said burglary, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Hnatyshyn):
That the Solicitor General, without any further delay, make a statement on motions outlining the government's intentions with respect to the implementation of Judge Rene Marin's report which will be to the benefit of the vast majority of the RCMP.

subsubtopic: DATE FORMER SOLICITOR GENERAL BECAME AWARE OF BREAK-IN AT L'AGENCE DE PRESSE LIBRE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I must say in reply to the question of the hon. member that, as he is aware, an official inquiry was launched as soon as my predecessor was advised of the break-in or presumed break-in at the offices of the APLQ. That judicial inquiry is still under way, Mr. Speaker, and as I indicated to the House during the oral question period last Friday, as soon as sentence is passed, that is as soon as the legal process has been completed, I shall make as complete as possible a statement to the House on all circumstances surrounding the case of the APLQ.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I gladly accept the minister's answer and will not ask more about the precise date on the understanding he will cover that point in his statement on the ninth. In view of circumstances involving one of the participants in this incident, and keeping in mind that I and some of my colleagues have often raised incidents in this House concerning RCMP officers who, owing to the arbitrary disciplinary procedures to which they are subjected, find themselves in difficulty, will the minister implement some of Judge Rene Marin's recommendations in the near future in order to put right inequities which, as I think the minister will agree, have caused the force much dissatisfaction within its ranks?
[ Translation]

Mr. Speaker, of course it is most unfortunate that doubtless because of his many preoccupations the hon. member was unable to attend the sitting of the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs which studied my budget last Thursday, because he could then have asked all those questions in detail. In any

event, Mr. Speaker, I can assure him that following really intensive consultations with the RCMP, consultations which ended at the end of last November with representatives of the constables and other non-commissioned officers of the RCMP, an internal committee of my department composed in part of RCMP representatives made a complete review of the recommendations of the Marin report. Since that time, several of Justice Marin's recommendations have been accepted by the RCMP; as for the others, Mr. Speaker, I am expecting a report from my department before the end of June and hope to be able to introduce appropriate legislation to the House during the next session of Parliament.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF FORECASTS OF LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT IN EACH PROVINCE-MEASURES TO REDUCE LEVEL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. Last Tuesday I asked the minister if he would confirm the existence of unemployment forecasts that were made by members of his department for the province of Quebec and other provinces. At that time the minister said he would look into the situation and report back. My question today is, will he now confirm that such forecasts were made by his department for the province of Quebec and other provinces? Will he table for the observation and scrutiny of members of this House the truly alarming figures that come out of those forecasts? Related to that, will he also advise if his department is planning any initiative to improve the unemployment situation in the next few years?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR TABLING OF FORECASTS OF LEVEL OF UNEMPLOYMENT IN EACH PROVINCE-MEASURES TO REDUCE LEVEL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can confirm that projections of various trends in the economy, including employment and unemployment, were recently published by the regional economists in Quebec. My understanding is that there was no authority to make this kind of information public. It is not our business to do that kind of forecasting. There are competent organizations, such as the Economic Council of Canada and the Conference Board of Canada, which make these projections. All of these sources are used by the department. We do not intend to make it a practice to publish these figures in the future, either for Quebec or other provinces.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the people of this country, particularly the provincial governments, have a real concern about these forecasts even if the minister does not. They are already available. subsubtopic: REASON FOR FAILURE TO CONSULT OTHER PROVINCES PRIOR TO AGREEMENT WITH QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct my question to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. Without having any prejudice as to the recent discussions the minister had with the minister in Quebec, I should like to ask him on what basis and what was the justification for making a new deal with the province of Quebec on immigration without first consulting the other nine provinces and the Parliament of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subsubtopic: REASON FOR FAILURE TO CONSULT OTHER PROVINCES PRIOR TO AGREEMENT WITH QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me first say there is no new deal with this particular province. We were talking about the selection of immigrants to Quebec and our discussions were based on section 95 of the British North America Act which indicates that this is an area of shared jurisdiction. It permits the

May 30, 1977

co-determination of both levels of government in the immigration selection process. When I was asked, in dealing with one province, whether this was something which was available to all other provinces, the answer was yes. At the present time we have two agreements with the province of Quebec. Similar opportunities have been made available to other provinces but they have not seen fit, for their own reasons, to take them up. The Bienvenue-Andras agreement was, as Mr. Couture indicated, a good step forward, but it seems now we can do more with respect to sharing or codetermining immigration designated for various parts of the country. We agreed to the establishment of a joint working group which will look into all the options available. This will be available not only to Quebec but to any province which wants to participate.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE FEDERAL CONTROL NOT RELINQUISHED TO PROVINCES
REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE FEDERAL CONTROL NOT RELINQUISHED TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I trust the minister will have full respect for freedom of mobility in Canada. Would he give an assurance to the House and to the Canadian people that the federal government will exercise majority influence over immigration rather than release it to provincial jurisdiction and thus threaten the opportunity for a sensible, rational immigration policy throughout Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE FEDERAL CONTROL NOT RELINQUISHED TO PROVINCES
speechtext: Both Mr. Couture and I share that concern. As a matter of fact, Mr. Couture suggested, if I may use his words, that at the federal level we ought to have a common denominator in order to preserve and protect that vital element of immigration policy in Canada, namely, a person's ability to move throughout Canada despite the fact that he might originally have been designated to go to one province. There was no suggestion of any breakdown in that regard.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE FEDERAL CONTROL NOT RELINQUISHED TO PROVINCES
speechtext: I am not sure whether the minister stated this categorically, but I just wanted him to state, in front of the House of Commons, whether the federal government got the say in more than 50 per cent of immigration policy? That is the simple question I would like the minister to answer.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE FEDERAL CONTROL NOT RELINQUISHED TO PROVINCES
speechtext: More important than getting into semantics over percentages, what we must look at is codetermination and the determinate role. Percentages are not going to make that amount of difference in numbers. It is a question of making sure that we maintain a common denominator and do what is necessary to encourage Francophone immigration to Canada as well as ensure the ability of the immigrant to move throughout the country.

cent of the points given to immigrants coming to Canada. I want to know from the minister whether he said no to that request and, if he did not say no, what did he say?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subtopic: QUEBEC REQUEST FOR CONTROL OF POINTS GIVEN PROSPECTIVE IMMIGRANTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Couture indicated he was interested in selecting the best formula that would meet both our requirements. If there is a better system, even beyond the pointage system, such as a sponsorship system or some other role that province might play, he wanted to look at all the options. That is why he agreed with me to establish a working group so that we could look not only at the options suggested by him but at others that we might wish to propose.

I take it from the minister's answer that his counterpart in Quebec has now abdicated with regard to that particular proposal. The minister can answer that question when I ask him my second question. I understand that in the minister's statement he advised his counterpart that the selection process can be divided into two parts, one affecting social, cultural and demographic aspects and the other concerned with economic and labour aspects as well as market conditions, the latter being the responsibility of the federal government. Was there any discussion with respect to that type of thinking on the part of the minister and, if so, what was the reply in that regard?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speechtext: I am not certain what the hon. member means in the first part of his question about abdicating or backing off.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, may I direct my question to the Acting Prime Minister because the matter I want to raise has to do with the government in general. Last Thursday in the House the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources stated that the government had made no decision with respect to the construction of a reprocessing plant to extract plutonium from radiation waste and to use that plutonium with thorium to provide electric energy for Ontario Hydro. I want to ask the Acting Prime Minister if the government's attention has been drawn to a press conference last Friday at which officials of AECL stated that it would be inappropriate to scrap the plans for a plutonium plant even if the government is opposed. May I ask the Acting Prime Minister also if he thinks it is appropriate that officials who are hired to advise the government on the nuclear energy policy should be publicly advocating a course of action on which the government itself has allegedly not yet made a decision?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Acting Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: ALLEGED STATEMENT CONCERNING ESTABLISHMENT OF PLANT TO PRODUCE PLUTONIUM-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Until the hon. member raised the question, to the best of my knowledge the attention of the government had not been drawn to the press conference. That is in answer to the first part of the question. If the story, as alleged by the hon. member, is correct, I will most certainly want to see the government question the propriety of any agency making a statement indicating its opposition or contradiction to or its disagreement with what appears to be the government's stated policy. But I would like to check what the hon. member has quoted, which he probably got from the press as well.

subtopic: SUGGESTED PUBLIC INQUIRY INTO USE OF NUCLEAR ENERGY
SUGGESTED PUBLIC INQUIRY INTO USE OF NUCLEAR ENERGY
speechtext:
In
view of the fact that modern science has given us tremendous powers which can be used for the benefit of or the destruction
May 30, 1977

of mankind, and in view of the fact that the nuclear advisers to the government are engaged in the business of selling nuclear reactors and technology, I want to ask the Acting Prime Minister whether the government is now prepared to consider the fact that the time is long overdue for Canada to follow the example of other countries, such as the United Kingdom which appointed a royal commission under Sir Brian Flowers, to assess the dangers and the benefits of nuclear energy and to come up with recommendations upon which Canada could base the same nuclear policy that would be in the public interest?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Acting Prime Minister):
subtopic: SUGGESTED PUBLIC INQUIRY INTO USE OF NUCLEAR ENERGY
speechtext: I would point out to the hon. member my own view that the government is totally aware of the potential dangers and it has these constantly under examination. In fact it is taking measures to make sure that the proliferation and sale of reactors is carried out under a sound and sane policy, as the hon. member suggests. As to whether it would be necessary for a royal commission to be struck to do this, that is a different question indeed, and I take that as a representation which no doubt will be noted.

subtopic: SUGGESTED PUBLIC INQUIRY INTO USE OF NUCLEAR ENERGY
speechtext: In view of the answer of the Acting Prime Minister I would like to point out that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said last Thursday that he had asked the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works to look into this matter, but, as every hon. member in the House knows, that committee has neither the time nor the expertise to examine a problem of such magnitude. I wonder if the Acting Prime Minister would undertake to discuss with the Prime Minister and his colleagues the fact that a reprocessing plant is not immediately necessary, and in light of that whether it would be preferred- because this has not been dealt with in any of the government's guidelines regarding the export of nuclear capacity-to examine the whole question of reprocessing plants by appointing a commission consisting of qualified scientists with no commercial bias in the hope that we might be able to establish guidelines for our domestic nuclear policy before we embark upon a course of action which could have disastrous effects not only on ourselves but also on future generations.

subtopic: SUGGESTED PUBLIC INQUIRY INTO USE OF NUCLEAR ENERGY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, obviously the hon. member is registering his concerns, and we should be listening to him. The hon. member made a representation which I will certainly ensure is carried forward for consideration. Beyond that I cannot give the hon. member a definitive answer.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prince Albert):
subsubtopic: SUGGESTION GRANTING OF POWERS TO QUEBEC SHOULD BE DEBATED IN HOUSE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question arises out of the initial questions to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. If I understood him correctly, he agreed that arrangements could be made between the federal and any provincial government-and other provin-

May 30, 1977
Oral Questions
cial governments would have the same right-to determine the question of immigration into their respective provinces. That to me is a proposition which is a denial of any concept of "one Canada". Would that not lead to a situation whereby any one province could say that whatever the other provinces said, "We do not want any French people migrating into this province; we do not want any English people migrating into this province; we do not want Jews in this province"? Is this not an outrageous proposition which will balkanize Canada? I suggest to the minister that this is too serious to leave to this government to come to an arrangement with the P.Q. government in Quebec. It is a matter which should be brought before the House of Commons so that we can find out the views of Canada and Canadians as a whole. Balkanization may meet a situation which exists today, but in the future it would be a denial of any expectation of greatness in the destiny of this nation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subsubtopic: SUGGESTION GRANTING OF POWERS TO QUEBEC SHOULD BE DEBATED IN HOUSE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I might agree with the right hon. gentleman if the points were being awarded on the basis of the criteria that he is suggesting. That might have the impact of balkanizing the country. I feel that we are dealing here with section 95 of the British North America Act, which makes provision for a co-determination of the landing of immigrants in this country. This has worked to the benefit of this country since it became a nation. I do not think anyone would deny that. We are attempting to live up to the spirit of the British North America Act, section 95, by saying to the provinces that it is conceivable that in the past the federal government has acted almost in a unilateral way by setting out the points system, by saying who would be allowed to come in and by letting immigrants settle wherever they please. Quebec and other provinces-

speechtext: What other provinces?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION GRANTING OF POWERS TO QUEBEC SHOULD BE DEBATED IN HOUSE

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION GRANTING OF POWERS TO QUEBEC SHOULD BE DEBATED IN HOUSE

Consultation, yes, but not outright acceptance of the viewpoint of the provinces. The minister believes discussions should take place, but does the minister not agree that the discussions should be held here in the House of Commons so that this matter can be determined as a result of the views of Canadians as a whole rather than those of the Prime Minister of Canada and the Premier of Quebec, who in the past were as close as two peas in a pod?

Mr. Speaker, I think the right hon. gentleman and I share the hope of the minister of immigration for the

province of Quebec that we do in fact maintain a Francophone immigration into this country. We have come up with suggestions and ideas in the past which have been adopted, and in two agreements entered into by predecessors of mine we have in fact recognized that. The fact that we spend money on advertising only for Francophone immigration was recognized, and in the interest of doing that which is good for Canada we are authorized under the statute to enter into individual agreements. subtopic: REQUEST FOR INCREASED ALLOWANCE FOR PARAPLEGICS AND QUADRAPLEGICS
REQUEST FOR INCREASED ALLOWANCE FOR PARAPLEGICS AND QUADRAPLEGICS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare relates to increased allowances for paraplegics and quadraplegics in this country. I realize the legislative aspect of the question at the moment. Can the minister inform the House if any special studies are going on at the present time in his department with regard to a special allowance for these people who are unfortunate enough to be confined to a wheelchair without the added cost of catheters and medication as well as the frustration of facing a wheelchair every day?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: REQUEST FOR INCREASED ALLOWANCE FOR PARAPLEGICS AND QUADRAPLEGICS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first of all, I am pleased to advise the hon. member that I hope to introduce in this House very shortly a new piece of legislation called the social services act which will have as one of its highest priorities the improvement of services to the handicapped in this country. As far as specific payments are concerned, such payments are authorized for cost-sharing under the Canada Assistance Plan but the provinces must take the initiative in deciding the level of payments with the federal government paying 50 per cent of what the program costs as determined by the provinces. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, may I direct my question to the minister responsible for answering. Canada, the great abstainer, abstained again on this matter. I should like the minister to explain why we abstained instead of voting against the draft article?

speakeroldname: Mr. Fernand E. Leblanc (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):

subsubtopic: REASON CANADA ABSTAINED FROM VOTING ON ARTICLE TO EXTEND RIGHTS OF PRISONERS OF WAR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this conference is to extend the protection afforded by the 1949 Geneva Convention to those affected by armed conflict. While Canada has actively supported the humanitarian aims of the conference, we abstained on this question, along with a number of other western delegations, since the terms of the article were highly ambiguous and could be interpreted to adversely affect the protection which is to be afforded to the civilian population during times of war.

May 30, 1977
Privilege-Mr. Paproski

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it seems that the difficulty which has been encountered in this case and encountered before could be remedied by the committee studying the rules and procedures of this House if it were provided in the Standing Orders that any member who wants to say no when a motion is introduced under Standing Order 43 be required to stand up and be recognized so that he is recorded in Hansard.

subsubtopic: MR. PAPROSKI-PROCEDURE IN DEALING WITH S.O. 43 MOTIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEEDS OF SMALL BUSINESS

speakeroldname: Mr. Otto Jelinek (High Park-Humber Valley) moved:
subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEEDS OF SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
That in the judgment of this House the Government has failed to respond effectively to the needs of the small business sector, has made negligible progress toward the implementation of a small business policy, has neglected to introduce a Small Business Act, and has not freed the productive potential of small business to create jobs for Canadians.
He said: Mr. Speaker, at the outset may I extend my sympathies to the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Marchand) on the death in his family. We all know the sadness that is felt when losing loved ones, and we share that sadness with him today.
It has been roughly one year since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) appointed a member to his Cabinet who would be responsible for looking after the interests of the small business community. At that time a glimmer of hope arose within this vast and major sector of our economy, a hope that at long last specific action would be taken to reduce the maze of bureaucratic regulations, controls, directives, and the general paper work onslaught would be replaced with a meaningful incentive oriented program.
Unfortunately nearly a year has passed and the small businessman still must look to a government that has no small business policy whatsoever let alone a small business act. He must still look to a government lacking meaningful incentive programs, and he must look at a minister who is attempting to work in a policy vacuum without any terms of reference with which to set his sights for the future.
That reminds me of a statement made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), who unfortunately is not in the Chamber today. When faced with the possibility of creating a language ministry, the minister refused such a proposal because the terms of reference were not worked out. One must wonder what the difference is between that proposed ministry and the appointment of a Minister of State responsible for small business when the terms of reference of that portfolio had not only not been worked out, but the minister has to work in a policy vacuum of sorts.

May 30, 1977
Small Business
In any event one must begin to wonder about the actual intent of the appointment. I had hoped that the government had at long last realized the necessity of dealing with small business as a separate entity, and that it was finally following in the footsteps of other industrialized nations that had been committed to the betterment of the small business community for some time. Consequently, their over-all economies are far healthier than our own.
Be that as it may, it is a fact that since the appointment of a Minister of State responsible for small business, the government's own attitude toward the small business sector has not changed. The government still does not have a small business policy. The government still does not have a small business act.
What is totally unbelievable and incredible is that the minister still does not have a definition of small business as it relates to his portfolio. How can you expect a government to deal with a specific sector of our economy when the government does not know exactly what sector it is dealing with?
There are a number of departments which deal directly or indirectly with small business. No wonder they are not helpful. No wonder they create bureaucratic paperwork and burdens, and impose all sorts of restrictions on the small business community. The departments cannot know where the line is drawn between large multinational corporations and small business. How can the government continue to pretend, and that is all it is doing, to be interested in this vital sector of our economy, small businesses, when it does not know who it is dealing with?
The minister just recently had the second reading of the Small Businesses Loans Act passed. I look forward to taking part in the committee stage debate on that bill tomorrow. However, it is nothing new. The act was implemented in 1963. This is just a continuation of that act. Hon. members know that act would have expired July 1 had amendments not been introduced.
The amendments do not go far enough. They simply keep time with inflation. Nothing has been done by the government to stimulate the small firms sector. No incentives programs have been established to extend the sector into secondary manufacturing. No effort has been apparent in utilizing this small business community for make-work programs, yet small business, which is responsible for over 50 per cent of the labour force in Canada, is the largest and least costly sector of potential employment opportunity within our economy as a whole. I want to emphasize that. Incredibly this is the one sector that the government continues to overlook when pretending to deal with unemployment.
During my recent trip to Tokyo where I held various discussions with officials of the small and medium size enterprise agencies, what hit me most vividly was the difference in priorities between the Japanese government and that of our own. In Japan, as in the United States, West Germany and elsewhere, governments have been catering to the well-being of the small business community over the past 20 years or so. As a result their economies are far more advanced than ours, especially when it comes to unemployment where, for example,

Japan has close to zero unemployment in a population of 110 million people while we have reached the frightening figure of one million unemployed in Canada. One of the main reasons for this imbalance in statistics is that we are not taking advantage of this, the best and cheapest potential job employment opportunities in a mixed economy-I keep referring to small business, of course.
Unfortunately the philosophies of the government over the past decade or so have tended toward centralization, with bigger and costlier governments, stronger and more powerful unions, and larger and fewer multinational corporations. It is my deep concern that unless this trend toward centralization does not reverse itself within the very near future, our system, the free market system upon which this country was built, will slowly but surely disappear to be replaced by what I can only describe as corporate socialism.
Let us remember that small business is the umbilical cord of free enterprise. The fact remains that our governments, despite this, continue to consult with large business and, as a result, most of the legislation is geared solely toward that sector. This forces small business to accept various laws which were not based on their problems in the first place. There is no question that the needs of the small corporation are largely different from those of the large multinational.
I turn to another subject, that of secondary manufacturing. We sometimes tend to forget that Canada is the richest nation per capita in natural resources, and even with that wealth, look at the state of our economy! One of the reasons we are doing so badly is that the government does not provide an incentive. It does not offer an incentive to industry to develop secondary manufacturing. We need the United States, as I have said in the past, to help us develop some of our natural resources.
But what concerns me, what should concern every member of the House, is that instead of continuing to sell our natural resources abroad where we help create employment, in Japan, for example, where we help the economies of foreign nations to develop on the basis of our natural resources as they develop secondary manufacturing to produce the final product, we lose that potential, that opportunity for employment in this country. Then we turn around and buy those finished products back from Japan, though very often they are made out of our own natural resources, at much higher cost. This is a situation which has to be faced by all Canadians and this trend of depending on foreign countries to develop and build their economies from our natural resources must be reversed because one of these days we are going to run out of natural resources, and then where are we going to be, with no secondary manufacturing?
If we want this trend to be reversed we must surely come up with an incentive program to assist the development of these vital secondary manufacturers, and instead of strangling the small business community with bureaucracy and all kinds of restrictions and controls it is time the government initiated forms of incentive, be they through the tax system, research
May 30, 1977

and development, or a number of other ways where incentives can be introduced. This would encourage the growth and development of small firms, thereby creating employment at the lowest possible cost. This simply is not happening.
To my mind, incentive is the key word and one which has disappeared from the political vocabulary of the government sitting across the way. Instead of incentive programs we are now in the midst of the greatest give-away era in our history. One must remember that the higher the number of direct grants or give-aways the less incentive there is for realistic productivity, just as the higher the number of unemployment benefits, the less incentive there is for long range employment.
This is not to say that less effort should be geared to the well-being of big enterprises and large multinationals. More often than not, however, these are able to fend for themselves. Indeed over the five years I have spent in Ottawa it has become obvious that the effect of a big business lobby on cabinet ministers and their departments can be compared to a tiger in a monkey cage. Whenever big business lobbies for its cause, ministers do back handsprings in an effort to be of assistance.
Unfortunately the small businessman does not have the clout or the resources to make himself heard effectively. Whatever ear-bending has been accomplished must be credited to such organizations as CFIB, the CMA and a few others. Unfortunately whatever success these groups may have had, or whatever success the opposition may have had in proposing realistic recommendations in this regard-and I say "proposing realistic recommendations" because we have done this on a regular basis ever since I have been here, especially in this field-has gone for naught. It is meaningless unless the government commits itself wholly to the betterment of the small business community.
Some of the recommendations we have made in the past were debated on March 28 of this year in connection with a private member's motion in my name. We talked about this subject at length. I shall be very brief. I shall simply call attention to the four points which were included in this motion; first, that tax credits should be allowed in respect of investment in small business. We. have been pushing for this since 1972, and not only the small business community but Canadians at large would accept it. But the government is dormant. It has a one-track mind, a preoccupation with bigness, big government, big unions, big labour. This is why unemployment is so high. This is why our economy is suffering. IThe second point was the need for assistance in the formation of small business export consortia. The third was the need for changes in government tendering practices so that small business would supply an increased proportion of government purchased goods and services. A program to this end has been most effective in the United States. The fourth point concerned the need to reduce the government paperwork burden imposed on small business.
With regard to the last point I must give credit to the Minister of State for Small Business. He has, finally, listened and taken some steps in this direction, though to date they are
Small Business
very hesitant. For example, the government has gone some way toward reducing the reporting requirements to Statistics Canada of certain firms in the construction, transportation and manufacturing industries. We look forward to further developments in this field and we look forward, as well, to the promised amendments to the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act which will exempt further firms having to report under that law. But this is barely scratching the surface. Each time the minister opens his mouth, on the other side he develops a bureaucratic maze with which small business must try to cope.
The government does not realize that whenever it introduces a piece of legislation dealing with business it places an unfair burden on smaller firms which very often have no relation to what is happening. I will give one example. Quotas are undoubtedly needed to assist the textile industry in Canada. But in introducing the measures it did, the government gave no thought to the little corner store which, for instance, was marketing Mexican novelty goods and was in no way trying to compete against the large textile manufacturers. Operations such as these are the ones which suffer from the kind of legislation to which I have referred. Their owners go bankrupt and employment is lost. This is happening on a daily basis. There are more bankruptcies taking place today in Canada in small business than ever before in our history. All of this indicates that the government does not care, does not understand, or does not want to care about implementing specific programs for large industry or planning specific programs for small business.
The minister himself cannot be blamed personally for attempting to deal with this issue.

1 am sure I do not have to remind hon. members of the importance of small business to our economy. Without a small business policy and a government commitment, by way of a small business act, this importance is being slowly but surely eroded and is perhaps damaging the free market system for good.
I would like to take this opportunity to quote from a report by the Select Committee on Small Business in the United States Congress. I keep referring to the United States because I feel this is one area of our economy where we can learn from something which has been successful, and we can learn from something which has existed for the last 30 years. It is unfortunate, but the government does not seem to want to learn. I would like to quote from page XI of the Permanent Select Committee on Small Business of the House of Representatives of the United States, which reads as follows: Importance and Place of Small Business in U.S. Economy.
The contributions of small business to the American economy and society are many and the following points merit special attention:

1.	The existence of a large number of small, independent businesses helps to preserve competition, thus ensuring increased efficiency and high quality and reasonable prices for consumers.
2.	A large number of small independent businesses decreases the likelihood of excessive economic and political control.
3.	Small business offers an opportunity for the expression and growth of personal initiative and individual judgment.
4.	Small business is frequently the source of new products and new methods.
5.	Small business constitutes a large and diversified source of employment opportunities.
6.	Certain services essential to the economy can be performed best by small business.
I wanted to quote from this report just to emphasize the importance of small business within our economic way of life. We have been calling for a government small business policy for years. We have been calling for the government to commit itself for the betterment of the small business sector for years. We have been calling for positive and specific programs, and none have been forthcoming. We have recommended in detail, on a number of occasions, specific proposals for the betterment of the small business community. Mr. Speaker, all of this was to no avail. Instead of acting positively in this regard, the government has ignored the needs of the small business sector. It has refused to implement a small business policy, let alone consider introducing a small business act. The resulting factors can be judged by the shape of our economy as a whole, which goes hand in hand with the deplorable level of unemployment in this country.
The time has come for specific and positive action. Therefore I am calling on the government through this motion today, as emphatically as I can, to introduce a small business act which would fall within the confines of a small business secretariat responsible for initiating and consequently updating, on a regular basis, a specific small business policy dedicated to the betterment and well-being of small and medium size enterprises in Canada.
The motion today records the failure of the government to present or even consider such a small business act. Mr. Speaker, I advocate such an act. After just speaking previously of the weight of government intervention upon small business, it may now seem strange to ask for what appears to be more regulation of small business through legislation; but the two goals are not inconsistent and are not contradictory. They are complementary, because one of the major goals of a small business act would be to remove, as far as possible, the weight of government upon small business and to assist small business in coping with government. I will make some more detailed suggestions in a moment.
First and foremost there must be a definition of what a small business is. If government is to prepare and implement any coherent program for small business, then it must first know, with some exactitude, what a small business is. The government talks about small business but does not know what small business is, because it does not have any government policy with respect to a definition. That does not seem very difficult, but so far the government has not come up with a definition that makes any sense to a small businessman.
May 30, 1977

The government definition of small business is based on size, the total assets of the firm or its gross sales in a year. Conceptually this definition is inadequate because it fails to capture the most important feature of a small firm-that the owner of it is the manager and that the manager of the firm has a deep personal stake in its future. The inadequacy of the definition, in its practical application, is easy to illustrate. Let me take one definition of small business which is based on size. That is contained within the Small Businesses Loans Act as it is proposed to be amended by Bill C-48. In that legislation a small business enterprise is defined as one which has an estimated gross revenue of $1.5 million in a year. According to this legislation, a small business is a firm having less than $1.5 million in sales.
Let us apply that definition to a few firms in Canada. I am not suggesting any of these firms which I will mention have applied for a small business loan or do not fall under the definition of this act specifically. Consider a company called Nordex Explosives Ltd., based in Montreal. Their sales in 1975 were $433,000. This company is safely under the small business sales limit of $1.5 million. Is this company in fact a small business? I would argue that it is not, and I think the major shareholder of the company, which happens to be the Dow Chemical Investment and Finance Corporation of Michigan, would be rather surprised to hear that a company they control is considered to be a small business by this Liberal administration. Dow Chemical's gross revenue exceeded $5.6 billion in 1976; it is twenty-fifth on the list of the top 500 U.S. corporations compiled by Fortune magazine.
I have a great number of other such examples where the government defines a so-called Canadian company within its own definition under the Small Businesses Loans Act, a company which is in fact held by multinationals from abroad or in Canada. The list is long. It is sufficient to show that the definition of a small or medium size business based on size alone does not always describe the most important feature of a small business, namely, that it is owner-managed.
Therefore the first thing our small business act must do is to define small business as an enterprise that is owner-managed. That is the main component of the United States small business act definition, and it seems to be workable. One may then want to apply a size limit to the companies identified by the owner-managed definition so that large owner-managed operations, such as Eaton's of Canada, are excluded, or to be more flexible one may choose to qualify the owner-managed definition with the requirement that the firm not be dominant in its field of operations or its market. The degree of dominance may seem to be a vague criterion, but it is one which in effect will be used in the proposed revisions of the Combines Investigation Act, Bill C-42. The precise qualifiers used are not as important as the main feature of the definition, that the enterprise be owner-managed.
Having made the definition workable in my view, as it has certainly been workable in the United States for some time, let
Small Business
us look briefly at the proposed act. The small business act would create a small business secretariat which would function independently of its parent, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Currently the small business responsibilities of the department are treated like a blemish on its plans for large scale operations, big plants, huge capital costs, and large scale exports. The concerns of small business are both different in quality and quantity from those of big business, so different, I would argue, that a small business secretariat could never be comfortable under the suffocating umbrella of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The secretariat's job would be to help small business cope with government and compete with big business.
I am not proposing government intervention in the affairs of small business, far from it. What I am proposing is a mechanism through which the weight of big government can be removed from the shoulders of small business.
The secretariat would have an advocacy role. By this I mean the secretariat would put forward the interests of small business to other government departments and agencies. I mentioned how many departments and agencies there are that touch on small business interests, or rather I would say that do not touch on small business interests because there is no department that is reorganized-

For example, when Statistics Canada is preparing yet another statistical form which requires a lawyer or an accountant to fill it out, the secretariat would try to force StatsCan to exempt small businesses from being required to complete it or, at the very least, would try to have the form simplified and streamlined. Another thing the secretariat might do is to make representations to the Department of Finance to try to prevent the implementation of budget proposals harmful to small business. This happens quite often without the knowledge of the top department that the legislation that is being proposed for the big multinational corporations is in fact harming small businessmen. I touched on that previously.
The secretariat also could make representations to the Metric Commission to ensure that conversion costs are not an undue burden on small business, or to the Export Development Corporation to ensure that small business gets a fair share of EDC financing and insurance contracts. The secretariat could make representations to any other department the actions of which affect the small firms sector. I could go on and on, but this will not work in Canada until such a policy is brought in under an act which would commit the government to deal specifically with the interests of small businesses rather than

May 30, 1977
Small Business
dealing with small businesses in a roundabout way through the various departments.
It has been proposed in Bill C-42, for example, that there be a competition advocate, so really I am not setting a precedent in recommending an advocate because the government itself has recommended an advocate under Bill C-42. The job of such a person would be to make representations to federal departments, agencies, and corporations whose actions affect competition in the market place. This is exactly what I am proposing for the benefit of the small businessman. All I am asking for is a small business advocate who may find it necessary, as part of his duties, to make representations to the competition board.
The secretariat will assist small business in forming export consortia. Such assistance will not only include the maintenance of files on businesses willing to form consortia, but will also include assistance in sales programs abroad. The secretariat will advocate, and perhaps institute in co-operation with other departments, a program whereby a certain portion of government purchased goods and services is supplied by small business-the set-aside program as it is called in the United States, to which I referred in my previous private member's motion in the House a month or two ago.
The small business act would transfer the administration of the educational function of the Federal Business Development Bank to the secretariat. The improvement of managerial skills is not something that is only needed when a small businessman needs to borrow money. It is a continuing need and should be a service available cheaply from the secretariat.
The small business act should amend other legislation. For example, it would be made perfectly clear that small business would be exempted from the sections of the new Competition Act dealing with specialization agreements, export specialization and mergers. Small business would be free from these rules and thus free from the fear of expensive and time consuming experiences before the competition board. Small business would not, of course, be exempted from the provisions dealing with misleading advertising or other unethical trade practices. In general, the small business act would exempt small business from regulatory statutes wherever consistent with other national goals. Small business has enough problems without bearing the weight of government.
Because time limitation will not permit me to deal with taxation proposals in this regard I will not speak about them at this time, but I hope that some of my colleagues will have an opportunity to touch on this subject. Let it not be said that we seldom make specific proposals and recommendations. I have been hinting at the need for a small business policy or act for some time, but the government obviously has not been interested in assisting the small business community. I had hoped that when the Minister of State for Small Business was appointed nearly a year ago, some action would be taken by the government, and some commitment made to deal with the problems of small businessmen, to come up with solutions. This has not happened.

On a number of occasions this year I put on the record some general proposals in this regard. For example, on March 28 of this year, as reported at page 4395 of Hansard, I said, and I quote:
Instead of the ad hoc, band-aid approach this government has taken in respect of small business, as indeed it has on a great number of other issues, a definite small business policy, or better still a small business act along the lines of that existing in the United States, Japan and elsewhere, must be established at the earliest possible date in order to replace the existing air of confusion, with potentially long-range programs.
I have made these recommendations on a number of other occasions both before and after March 28. Support for such action is not promoted simply by the Progressive Conservative Party. As a matter of fact I believe such action would be welcomed by a majority of Canadians. In fact the most effective voice of the small business community today, the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, utilizes the front page of its latest issue of Mandate to promote and thereby endorse our recommendation for a Canadian small business act.
I wish to quote briefly from the May issue of Mandate.

The quotation to which I would like to refer came after we made these recommendations publicly in this House and outside this House. It reads as follows:
In the United States, a national small business program has existed for almost three decades. Because of the Small Business Act, one third of federal spending for goods and services goes to small business. Since the United States has a program to benefit small business, it can hardly object to a similar Canadian program. Imagine what a larger small business sector would mean to Canada: more jobs, less need to import, retention of profits in Canada, and accumulation of valuable technological know-how. There's really no question. Canada must pass legislation committing the federal government to building domestic enterprises using the same wording and definitions as the U.S. Small Business Act. It seems to us that it's time Canada adopted something from the U.S. that makes sense for a change.
It went on to say, "The point is simple. We need a small business act now". We can see that the Canadian Federation of Small Business supports our recommendation.
In closing I would like to repeat what I have said often in this Chamber, something which I believe is imperative if our democratic way of life is to survive. If we want the small business firm sector to survive within our society, as I am sure we all do, then immediate action must be taken by the federal government. The small business community is what the free enterprise system is all about. It is what this country is built on and what this country can prosper by. Other countries which presently are more fortunate than Canada with respect to unemployment, inflation, productivity, and other areas by which the standard of success is judged, have all concentrated their economic energies toward their small firms sector within their industrial way of life.
My concern is so genuine regarding the problems of small business and freedom of enterprise that I hope the seriousness of these problems can be dealt with on a non-partisan basis. We cannot wait any longer, the small business community cannot wait any longer, and Canadians cannot wait any longer for the government to move in a positive direction in this regard. I hope hon. members will realize the seriousness of the situation and consider some of the proposals which we are outlining today. Opportunities still exist in Canada, but they are diminishing very quickly. Let us not lose them completely.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with fascination to the remarks of the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) concerning small business because, in my opinion, we cannot have capitalism and free enterprise as we have it today without having monopoly corporations, chain stores, and the largeness of industry which is supported by both the Liberals in Ottawa and the Conservatives in Ontario, without the elimination of small businessmen. 1 was fascinated because in the last few months I have been listening to the representatives of the Conservative Party in Ottawa talking about the need of additional funds for business. What they are talking about is big business. They are talking about the seven sisters in the oil company field. The Conservatives want to give them more money, and say they can develop because they are the only ones which produce jobs.
It is a fact that capitalism is no longer a free, competitive enterprise in Canada. The small businessman is affected by
Small Business
monopoly capitalism. It seems to me that while smallness is not necessarily beautiful, bigness is obscene.
I agree that this country was built by small businessmen, but they were competitive. They did not believe in monopoly capitalism. In my opinion the Federation of Independent Business is totally misdirected. I would have been more sympathetic to the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley if he had not cited the Federation of Independent Business to buttress his remarks. This federation has spoken in Mandate about every free enterprise exercise which has taken place for a long time, but in my opinion it is not in the least sympathetic to the small management operated business.
The Conservative Party here in Ottawa and in Ontario have recently been talking about the needs of the consumer and damning agriculture for its adherence to marketing legislation. Farmers are small, independent businessmen who have to get together to sell their products, but this is being attacked as being a very detrimental tool as far as the consumer is concerned.
The expression "free free enterprise" has been used. This seems to work for very large companies but never for the small ones. Let us consider an example. I am in total agreement with the remarks of the hon. member with regard to this country having been built by free enterprise. The businessman got an idea, he worked hard to sell it, he supplied a product, and in this way had people buying his "better mouse trap". That is not true anymore. Today if a businessman gets a good idea, somebody buys it and may use it to the advantage of the country or to the advantage of industry. On the other hand they may just shelve it because they already have a similar product, and so they eliminate the competition.
It is my opinion that free enterprise was intitially competitive enterprise. I should like to ask the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley what competitive enterprise he sees in the remarks made by the Federation of Independent Business? They no longer believe in competition; what they believe in is big conglomerates, with complete control. This control filters down to the small businessman. A little grocery store may order five or six cases of coke, and because of their low overhead, be able to sell it at less than other stores. This is fine. But they will find it impossible to get a second shipment of coke. If they do not sell at the right price the first time there will be no more deliveries of coke, Kraft products, or any other major commodities. That means there really is no competition.
What happens, say, to a small trucker in Ontario who finally can afford two or three trucks? He immediately finds that he comes under the control of the provincial government which will make it very difficult for him to expand. No protection is provided to the small free enterpriser to allow him to grow. He is regulated so that the competition factor limits his ability to expand because of government intervention.

That is a lot of nonsense.

May 30, 1977
Small Business

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEEDS OF SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
The hon. member says that is nonsense. There was a trucker in northern Ontario recently who had a small business. The government intervened and created a new class "A" licence. With the exception of the provincial government there have been no newly created class "A" PCV licences in my part of the country for the last eight or nine years. The recent one was a political move, and it may or may not be successful.
Small businessmen are the basis of our nation and they should be able to compete. In many cases they can only compete if they form a relationship with their neighbours. This is true in agriculture and in many other endeavours as well. It seems to me that governments are not very friendly to the relatively small businessman. It is much easier to deal with large gasoline companies than it is with the local service station, for instance. It is very easy to make arrangements on a provincial or federal basis with the seven sisters of the oil companies, but very difficult to make arrangements with the individual gasoline pump operator. So we see a diversity of prices across areas, that are quite often arranged prices. This happened in my area, particularly in Timmins which falls in a different zone than the rest of northern Ontario and has a different price base. It is not that the dealer has raised his price beyond what his overhead requires; it is that the price he pays for his product is different from what his neighbour pays in another zone in the same area.
The small businessman always gets it in the neck. Those who are considered small businessmen in agriculture are now faced with as much red tape as would be involved in running a major corporation. When they hire help they have unemployment insurance red tape, compensation red tape, income tax red tape and all the other forms of red tape, but there is no assistance available from the government. That is why many members of parliament get involved with the small business in their area; people are unable to cope.
In my area a number of people began to hire two or three employees but they found so much difficulty with the red tape that they got out of business. In New Liskeard two or three people got together and set up a small business-some were in the appliance business, some in television and radio-and together they hired one employee. They might as well have hired 100, Mr. Speaker. They were immediately involved with income tax, filling out forms, and shortly afterwards they dissolved the partnership because it just was not worth while. They are operating individually again, but they wanted to build a business that would have been an asset to the community and would have been advantageous to them because they had intended to share many facilities that are expensive to maintain individually.
Then there was a carpenter who decided to hire three or four people and build houses. The results were disastrous, not in terms of the buildings but because of the paperwork.
Any government that is really interested in helping small business-and I suggest the Conservatives in Ontario are not, and neither are the federal Liberals-should establish a bureau which would supply assistance in coping with red tape.
[Mr. Peters.)
As I have shown, when a small business wants to hire extra employees it would need the assistance of tax advisers and accountants.
I would say that small business should not go beyond the owner-manager category. It should be a stage between the private employer or contractor who is self-employed and the firm that goes into contracting and hires employees. Whatever bureau is established provincially or federally should be geared toward eliminating red tape. In every area of Canada it is essential to have an owner-managed grocery store or a hardware store operated by a local family. Our butchers must be allowed to run small or independent meat markets.
Our small businessmen are essential for the life of our communities. They are part of our way of life. It is no good paying lip service to small business; we must be prepared to help it. We should establish in the appropriate ministry a bureau which could help small business in exactly the same way as other government agencies help big business. If we are not willing to do it, we had better stop paying lip service to our free enterprise system.
To me, free enterprise means competitive enterprise. It means the world beating a path to the door of the man who builds a better mouse trap. I say this country's two major parties have not supported the builder of the better mouse trap for a long time. They have supported monopoly capitalism, have given concessions to large corporations, even in agriculture, where large business has secured monopoly control through vertical integration, and paid lip service only to the ability of the individual, of the small businessman, to compete effectively in the market place.
The small businessman thinks that he can compete only if he joins some larger organization which would allow him entry to the market place. With whom is the small businessman competing? A small businessman can go into the hardware business reasonably easily, but will find it difficult to stay afloat, if one of the large chain hardware stores opens business across the street. The large store can offer loss leaders, buy supplies in carload lots cheaply, and offer retail prices below those the small businessman must pay his supplier for the same goods.
I believe in the free, competitive enterprise system, but do not believe the Federation of Independent Business serves free enterprise. It serves big business or monopoly capitalism which allows no competition or squeezes or eliminates from the market any existing competition. When competition is eliminated we all become the victims. When most of us think of free enterprise, we think of competition.
I am sure most members of the House are aware of the problems besetting small business. I am sure lawyers, accountants, and others who deal with small business are aware of many problems our small businessmen must surmount in order to survive. Mr. Speaker, our small businessmen are important to our country. They are part of our way of life and we must support them. We must make sure our small businesses loans legislation works effectively.
May 30, 1977

If the newly appointed minister responsible for small business does his job properly and helps small businesses survive, perhaps small business will be given the sort of help the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and other agencies of government have given big business in the last few years. At present if a small businessman cannot borrow money from the bank under the small businesses loans legislation, he cannot borrow it anywhere. That is not good enough. I suggest we should involve the Federal Industrial Development Bank. At present I believe it is involved with those in medium-size enterprises.
Small businesses are labour intensive, community oriented, and make life for people in rural Canada and small communities more tolerable. Frankly I am surprised at the number of small businessmen who have joined the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, for as I see it the federation represents big business. It interests me to read reports published by the federation and compare the size of some of its member organizations. On the one hand you may have a plant employing up to 500, and on the other a small business with two or three employees. I often wonder why small businessmen think they are in the same category as the large corporation and why their sympathies are not with the independent people in their areas who support them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are dealing today with a motion concerning assistance to small business. I am pleased that such a motion has been tabled in the House and I congratulate the Progressive Conservative Party for having instigated that debate today. Someone said a while ago that it was small business which first took part in the birth, as it were, of the regions but in my opinion, it is the middle term between the state corporation and the great monopolies which I define as state capitalism and private capitalism.
It is not enough to establish a department for trying to protect small businesses. In fact this department has been in existence for one year and we have not heard of anything yet. In the past before this department was established, we tried our luck with the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) who was doing his best, I want to believe, trying to offer some help to small businesses, but I think too much emphasis was laid on helping large businesses.
Specially in our region we realize millions were given to large businesses, whether for research or for launching some large industries. Well, millions were sunk in large businesses, and small businesses were completely forgotten, to such a degree that I myself often worked with some people in my riding trying to gain acceptance for small businesses which would have been very profitable in a given town or sector, but we never could meet the blessed criteria specified by technocrats. And I believe it is at this stage that it is difficult for a small business to survive among the monopolies I mentioned a while ago. Today, of course, we are living in an era of monopolies and someone who has been in business for about
Small Business
forty years as I have has to realize that approximately 80 per cent of all businesses which were very viable forty years ago have been swallowed up by big monopolies.
For instance, about fifteen bakeries were in operation in my area some thirty years ago and they were all doing good business. Today there is only one bakery which is almost a multinational so that we must drive 125 miles to get bread. This whole bakery monopoly has paid the high price to get all those local bakeries closed and, after paying this high price, everybody said that if there were a larger market the retail price would improve. But the monopoly sets retail prices so no wonder everything is increasing, no wonder we have run-away price inflation. The main reason is monopoly control which is exercised in both industrial and commercial fields, as well as in the service area. Today, we even have all kinds of monopolies. The employment monopoly will be a reality within a few years, I believe, and we shall continue to live through this war of monopolies. The government must move immediately in an attempt to revive private enterprise which acts as a kind of screen to protect the consumer against these big monopolies which can overnight indicate the price they will impose on the consumer.
I think it is the duty of governments, not only the federal government but every government, to help small business not only through the creation of a ministry but also by passing legislation that will protect and encourage the small business sector. Some time earlier we mentioned small business loans. Those loans are not interesting for small business because of their high interest rate. For instance, the Industrial Development Bank, the Federal Business Development Bank is there to help enterprise.
But I have realized that this bank was there to help small business to die. We know that this bank helps small businesses only when they have been refused a loan by all other banks, all other loan institutions. When they must go to the Federal Business Development Bank they have to pay prohibitive interest rates when this bank, if it really exists to help small business, should ask only 50 per cent of the current interest rate. We might say that it would help small business but precisely because that small business, and I might give you some concrete examples, has been refused a loan by all other banks and loan institutions its credit gets a poor rating. It is the same for a business as for an individual. Today, someone who has a bad credit rating is going to pay 2, 3 or even 4 per cent more than someone with a good credit rating. That is sheer nonsense! Because an individual has more difficulty to pay than his neighbour he will be charged double interest. He has difficulties to earn his living, he has a small salary and this is because of our legislation, Mr. Speaker. He is charged 4 or 5 per cent more than the borrower with a regular job because his credit is bad.
If we really had legislation to protect consumers, we should charge the family head, that worker with a small income, 4 or 5 per cent less than those who can pay. It would be logical.

And to show you how we can live in illogically thinking we are in the best of worlds, that is in the legislation and regulations concerning financing plans, loan institutions and banks. If is the same for small industry: because it cannot benefit from large financing programs to obtain discounts, it has to pay 2, 3 or 4 per cent more than the medium-size industry which finds it easier to face those disbursements. This is why, Mr. Speaker, I am pleased we are discussing this matter today.
Indeed, I have before me a brief submitted to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, in which it is stated:
In submitting these representations, our aim is to refute any concept that small industries are less important or productive.
Small industry is praised for being the biggest employer, but the way things are now going, very soon it will no longer be so because it will be left to die. The brief goes on to say:
In view of the fact that small and medium factories account for 80 per cent of Canadian secondary industry, there is no doubt that this sector deserves serious consideration. In the context...
-because the brief was submitted to the committee that is scrutinizing Bill C-26 to give technical or other help to Canadian industries-
In the context of Bill C-26, the apparent theme is that universities alone are capable of creative theoretical research.
And as far as small industries are concerned, big corporations are given millions and millions of dollars for research. But often a fraction only is spent on actual research, and the government is not in a poslition to inspect those corporations' books. Small industries on the other hand would need help for research or administration or orientation, they could use a few thousand dollars to modernize, to stay afloat and face competition, but to my knowledge not a penny has been going their way in respect of research. I submit the government is at fault there for not giving small industry at least as much attention as it is giving big industry, because big industry, monopolies can look after themselves. I am still trying to figure out why the government keeps on giving grants for research or environment protection, let us say to forest industries or manufacturing industries that polluted everything. After they did the damage, the taxpayers' dollars are used to clean their mess.
If the government has millions of dollars to give large companies to repair the damage they have done to the environment, it should use this money to help our small industries and our small businesses which have a hard time surviving compared with supermarkets which can dictate their own conditions to the producers. I have often seen potato producers sell to a supermarket for 30 per cent less than the price they would have asked retailers because the supermarkets had the capital required and controlled all the local supply. They simply gave the producer the price they wanted to pay for his products.
That is what is wrong with those large monopolies. The ordinary retailer buys from the producer at the market price and, if you figure it out, he often still sells at a lower price than the supermarket because he does not have to pay all the publicity and the additional salaries that the supermarket must

pay to promote its products and pay for its packaging. Consumers should go around the small, well-organized grocery stores or well organized butcher shops. People are talking nowadays, especially in Quebec, about closing the small slaughterhouses. I for one believe that those small slaughterhouses should have a "Canada Approved" federal license and should stay open. I have been buying meat from a small slaughterhouse for 30 years. That is where you can find the meat and the quality you want, because you cannot find it in a supermarket and even less in regional slaughterhouses where you do not know what is going on or what kind of meat you are buying.
When there was all that talk about tainted meat, it was not in the small slaughterhouses that this meat was found, Mr. Speaker, but in the large ones. Today, because of the influence of these large monopoly slaughterhouses, the small slaughterhouses, that have always respected the life of the consumer, may finally disappear. Mr. Speaker, I am quite pleased that this problem should be discussed today and I hope the government will soon introduce legislation, not legislation to give strict directives to small businesses but legislation to protect them against those big monopolies, and I hope that legislation will be introduced by the next government as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, it was with great surprise that my colleagues on this side read the motion put forward today condemning the government in relation to what is taking place in a particularly healthy sector of the Canadian economy, namely, small business.
Hon. members opposite could have chosen to debate great issues. They could have spoken about ways in which to create more employment, or addressed themselves to the question of the incentives which ought to be left in the private sector to help the unemployment situation and fight inflation. My colleague the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Marchand) was appointed eight months ago. He has since travelled across Canada, meeting systematically and with a great deal of seriousness and concern representatives of small and medium-size businesses of the world. 1 personally joined him on several of those meetings in Ottawa when official groups representing those businesses were down here voicing problems covering all the difficulties small and medium-size Canadian businesses can be faced with and which, surprisingly, can include matters as varied and as absent from the speeches of those who spoke before me as the problem of inequities in the tax law which for the moment does not allow partners in small unincorporated businesses-usually the wife-to receive a salary from her husband.
