speechtext:
May 30, 1977
Small Business
realize that dream in the face of any obstacle. We honour that spirit. It is the aim of this government to see that it flourishes and prospers. The small business operator must be allowed to exercise his spirit of free enterprise to increase production and provide employment.
The government has taken some immediate steps since the Speech from the Throne to benefit the small operator. The recent budget contained a package of measures directed at encouraging small enterprise. We have begun to cut down the mass of paperwork which federal bureaucracy, in conjunction with provincial administrations, imposes on small business. Hon. members will know that there is a bill currently before the House to extend and increase the provisions of the Small Businesses Loans Act. The incentive and adjustment programs of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce have been amalgamated and redesigned to make them more accessible and more useful to the small business community.
The officials of the small business secretariat within the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce have been accumulating and studying the data on the state of small business in Canada today, in preparation for the over-all policy which my colleague, the Minister of State for Small Business, will be presenting to the government in draft form this summer. It is too early to state now what the elements of that policy will be. But I would like in these remarks to outline some of the basic directions in which our research into the small business community's present status has led.
First, however, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say clearly that the facts show that small business in Canada is not in bad shape, despite what some hon. members on the other side of this House would have us believe. The entrepreneurial spirit is alive and well in Canada, and it is making strides. Anyone who says that it is not is downgrading the ability and enterprise of Canadian small operators. Canada's small businessmen and women are holding their own in comparison with their counterparts in other countries. In our large cities and in our small towns Canadian entrepreneurs are showing that, given the chance, they can make the grade. It is the government's intention to give them that chance.
Some of the past and present initiatives of the federal government have been helpful to small business. The Federal Business Development Bank has made current commitments for $1.5 billion in loans to small and medium-size firms. At an average of $46,000 per loan the FBDB has helped a lot of businesses which would not otherwise have found the financing they needed. Some, but not enough, small Canadian Manufacturers have benefited from innovation and adjustment assistance programs of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Now that we have amalgamated many of these programs into one enterprise development program, I expect that even more assistance will be available to smaller firms.
The lion's share of assistance under the "alphabet soup" programs, such as PEP, IDAP, and the like, has too often gone to big companies. To give a giant corporation a government grant of $300,000 for innovative research is not the most effective way of using that money. To a company that size,

$300,000 is just peanuts. If they contemplate a research project, that contribution from government is not going to be the deciding factor in whether they go ahead or not. From observing the city of St. Leonard in my riding, which has a huge, new industrial park, a grant of $20,000 to a small firm can be the difference between trying something new or killing the project. If we took that $300,000 and broke it up, we could give $20,000 grants to 15 small firms, which could really stimulate some development and some jobs. This is the rationale behind the new enterprise development program: to redirect the assistance to small firms and get the most value out of federal funding for the small business community and for the country as a whole.
The program is to be administered by enterprise development boards in each province. These boards will have decisionmaking power on projects of up to $200,000 in federal assistance. To make sure that the boards are responsive to local business conditions, and to give them closer ties with the business community, their membership contains strong representation from the private sector, and the chairman of each board is a businessman, not a public servant.
At this point let me just correct one of the assertions of the hon. member who spoke before me who stated that a separate department and special act are needed to protect small businessmen and to give them better representation. This is not so. That would be to ghetto-ise them, and none of us want that. Instead, at the instigation of my colleague, the Minister of State for Small Business, several of us have started to review the composition of the various advisory boards and councils attached to our respective departments, and I for one have already directed my department to include representatives of small businesses on the advisory board counselling the two wings of my own department.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEEDS OF SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEEDS OF SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Among other recent measures beneficial to small business are those which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) brought down in the budget of March 31. The budget contained a package of measures designed to improve the climate for small business.
We propose changing the tax laws that govern employee stock options. Under the old system the difference between the market price of shares in a company and the price that the employee paid was immediately taxable as income.
This was quite a disincentive for employees to accept stock as part and parcel of an employment agreement. But under the new system in the March 31 budget, the difference between market price and the option price will be taxed as a capital gain-and not until the employee actually sells the shares. This will allow small Firms to offer stock as an attraction to first-rate, skilled people they would like to get into their businesses. It will give the smaller firms a better competitive edge in being able to get good management and skilled help of people who might otherwise go for the larger salaries that
May 30, 1977

bigger companies and government can offer. If the employee has a direct stake in the firm he works for, he is more likely to put out his fullest effort in the interest of the company.
Another feature of the budget which will help small business has to do with the treatment of gains on certain Canadian investments under the Income Tax Act. An investor, when he puts his money into a Canadian firm, will now be able to notify my department, Revenue Canada, that he wants any return on his investment to be treated as a capital gain rather than treating it as straight income.
The investor will be able to exercise this option once in respect of all his investments in certain Canadian securities. This is a lifetime option that, once exercised, is permanent.
This will aid small business by attracting more small, ordinary taxpayers as investors. Having the return on investment taxed as a capital gain rather than as income represents a considerable tax advantage. I think it will encourage a lot of venture capital firms to get behind Canadian small business. Of course this provision is not available to banks, credit unions, dealers in securities, or similar interests.
The tax regulations are also being changed to make it easier for one company to invest in another. The aim of this move is to encourage joint ventures between small firms. They will be able to get together to tackle larger projects which they could not handle on their own.
Another item in the budget which will benefit small business is the tax deferral on the voluntary sale of a firm's assets when they are being sold as part of a relocation. If a small firm closes down its operation in order to relocate in a better area, for example, there would be a deferral of capital gains tax on the sale of the firm's assets if the proceeds were invested somewhere else, in a similar business.
I have often heard small operators complain that they would like to move closer to sources of supply or relocate to take advantage of a better market, but they are held back by the penalty of taxes. These new provisions in the budget will help.
Apart from the items in the budget directly aimed at helping small business, there are some general measures which will indirectly benefit small firms. Retailers, for example, will like the change in tax regulations regarding inventory adjustments. In calculating business income, three per cent of the opening value of qualifying inventories-which means stock on the shelves on January 1-will be an allowable deduction. This benefit is available to unincorporated as well as incorporated businesses.
As well, the 5 per cent investment tax credit is being extended, and increased in slow growth areas. Current and capital expenditures for scientific research and development will be eligible for this credit. Many small Canadian firms are now doing good work in developing new technologies, and we want to encourage them.
Many of the measures contained in the budget respond to concerns expressed by small businesses themselves. They have also expressed other concerns and problems with the federal government.
Small Business
It is often said, for example, that small business cannot get close to government. It cannot find out what programs exist to benefit the small operator, because there are too few channels of communication. We want to improve communications and get the small entrepreneur into closer touch with assistance he could be getting from the federal government. I am hopeful that the Federal Business Development Bank, which has demonstrated a great deal of flexibility and creativity in its relations with small business, will be able to assume a substantial role in achieving that goal.
A good example of the kind of useful service the FBDB can offer to small business is the CASE program. CASE stands for counselling assistance for small enterprise, and it is basically an effort to provide small business with expert management and financial consulting services at a nominal cost. Many small business operators do their planning and accounting on the back of an envelope. And they make mistakes. They over-extend themselves. Or they leave out some important factors in their calculations. By the time they come to the FBDB or some other agency for help, it is often too late.
The CASE program is aimed at preventing that kind of business tragedy. CASE has a roster of hundreds of retired business people-those who have been through the whole routine and know the ropes. For a nominal amount of $20 per day, these retired business experts will come in and look over an operation and give a full report and advice on how to deal with any problem the business is facing.
These retired business people have an enormous collective expertise and business know-how. They volunteer for CASE because they really just want to stay involved with the business world. They like to keep in touch, and they like not having their accumulated expertise and experience go to waste.
Small business needs more risk financing from the FDBD. The bank therefore has been advised to provide more money in equity and loans to firms willing to take a risk on a good idea. Innovation always entails some element of uncertainty, but that should be no penalty to the small operator who wants to create something new.
Small business people have said that they would like an expansion of the provisions of the Small Businesses Loans Act. That act was passed in 1960 as a means of providing small business with loans from the chartered banks guaranteed by the federal government. Unfortunately, although the intention was good, the program has not worked as well as small business, the banks, and the government hoped it would. Fixed interest rates, often below the bank's prime rate, did not encourage the banks to lend under the act. It was costing them just as much to service these Small Businesses Loans Act accounts, but they were not getting as much return on their money.
Many small business people have said that they were not even aware of the provisions of the Small Businesses Loans Act. Their bankers simply never mentioned the program to

May 30, 1977
Small Business
them. I do not think the banks were at fault. Rather, it was the program which was not working.
This very week the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs will consider Bill C-48, which was referred to the committee on May 6. The committee will consider this bill, which is to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act and two related statutes governing farm and fisheries guaranteed loans. The amendments reply directly to many of the concerns raised by small business people. They have asked that the eligibility limit be raised from its present ceiling of $1 million in annual sales. We are therefore proposing to raise that limit to $1.5 million.
Small business people have asked that the limit on individual loans be raised from the present $50,000. We are therefore proposing to raise that limit to $75,000. We are also increasing the pool of money available for guarantees to $600 million from $300 million, doubling it.
We want to change the interest rate so that it floats with the banks' prime rate. Interest rates for these loans will be a little higher than prime, which will encourage the banks to start using the provisions of the program. We have discussed this matter with the chartered banks, and they have assured us that once these provisions will go through they will be happy to start making money available to small business under the terms of the act.
The Canadian Federation of Independent Business, chambers of commerce and the Canadian Manufacturers Association have all supported the proposed amendments. Once these changes in the legislation are in place, I think that the financial picture for small business people looking for risk financing should be brighter.
One of the complaints frequently heard from small business people is about the sheer volume of paper work which the small operator has to contend with for the federal government. We have made progress in reducing this volume of government paper work by getting the departments to share more information among themselves and by changing the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act. Because of these changes we will be exempting some 350,000 firms from at least one of their present reporting requirements by the end of 1981. We still have a long way to go, but our officials have calculated that the total dollar value to small business of the time saved in filling out these forms will be more than $40 million. Cutting back on paper work in this way, as I stated rather impatiently earlier on this afternoon, is a way to save money. These obsolete forms no longer have to be handled by programmers and clerks, and they do not have to be processed through expensive computers.
These are just some of the things we are doing right away, in advance of the policy paper to be considered by the cabinet this summer.
I should like to outline roughly some of the observations the government has made in studying Canadian small business with a view to shaping a federal policy toward the small entrepreneur. A primary observation is that small business

makes an essential contribution to the social and economic health of the country and, of course, of the various regions as well. I would like to point out that 98.6 per cent of all Canadian corporations-all those with assets under $5 million-are small or medium sized businesses. In the service industry, which has been the fastest growing sector of our economy in the past 30 years, small outfits overwhelmingly predominate. In construction, 99.5 per cent of all corporations are small, and together with unincorporated firms-individuals working on their own-they account for a very large share of the profits made.
In terms of employment, 91 per cent of all Canadian firms have 100 employees or fewer. Small business people and their employees account for one half the corporate wage bill in Canada.
Another observation is that social and economic changes in our country and in the rest of the industrialized world are making smaller units of production in the manufacturing sector increasingly more attractive. This process should result in more sub-contracting from larger firms to small companies, or it could mean more decentralization of larger firms.
Earlier this afternoon I was reading a very interesting speech which was made by the Minister of State (Small Business) to the Vancouver Board of Trade on March 21 when he was touring the country and meeting with as many representatives of the small business community as he could. Lie spoke at length about the decentralization of larger firms. I think he referred to the model which we are borrowing from Japan.
When we observe how the small operator relates to government, we find that existing government efforts to assist him may not suit his style. The entrepreneurial spirit and the kinds of attitudes which predominate in the public service do not always blend together well.
Another observation is that there is room for improvement in the way programs are delivered to the business community from government. All the various programs can be confusing to the businessman, particularly to the small operator who does not have expensive consultants to sort out things for him. I hope we can develop more federal-provincial co-operation in this area.
Whatever these preliminary observations on the state of small business may lead to in terms of the policy paper which will be brought to cabinet, they do tend to show that any government programs specifically intended to assist the small business community should be very decentralized and should have a major degree of participation from the private sector.
Through the forthcoming policy on small business in Canada the government intends to meet its responsibility to the small entrepreneur so that the best of free enterprise will flourish and prosper.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to the minister, and perhaps it might be
May 30,1977

a good idea to remind the Elouse of what is contained in the motion brought forward by the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek), which I had the honour to second.
It is obvious, judging by the minister's remarks-which I suppose were prepared by the same speech writer who prepared the famous $1,900 speech of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), and which said just about as much-that she neglected to read the motion. It is obvious that she did not see the order paper because she did not address her remarks to the terms of the motion. At the beginning of her remarks she said she could not understand why we brought forward such a motion; I will read it so that she will understand. The first part of ministerial understanding is to understand what she is talking about.
The motion begins as follows:
That in the judgment of this House the Government has failed to respond effectively to the needs of the small business sector ...
If the minister goes out into the street and talks to business people she will learn that the government has indeed failed to respond effectively. People are not going to be satisfied with all that ministerial pap we heard just a few moments ago, which was canned somewhere deep in the bureaucracy and regurgitated here in the House of Commons.
The motion continues:
-has made negligible progress toward the implementation of a small business policy ...
That is what the Canadian Federation of Independent Business has been saying about the government for years-that its policies have not been related to small business which provides 50 per cent of the employment in this country, but have been related to the needs of the large conglomerates and others. The minister would know that if she had read anything published by that organization, because that is the message they have tried to get through to the government. The motion continues:
-has neglected to introduce a Small Business Act...
And that is true. The Canadian Federation of Independent Business made representations to the Senate Committee on Foreign Affairs on May 26. I do not think the minister can have read the minutes of that meeting before she made her speech today. They pointed out that a small business act had not been introduced by the government and that it is a very serious omission. Before the minister speaks in this House again on the subject of the needs of small business she should read the testimony of Mr. Bulloch who appeared before that committee and set forth the desires of small businessmen.
The motion ends with the words:
-and has not fed the productive potential of small business to create jobs for Canadians.
That is obvious. Surely the government owes more to parliament and the people of this country, to the one million unemployed, to the Economic Council of Canada who predicted that, to the Canadian Federation of Independent Business,
Small Business
to the Board of Trade and others to which she gave lip service, than to have the minister stand in this House and attempt with nonsense to defend the policies of this government which are indefensible.
The minister talks about the "entrepreneurial spirit" in this country. It is there, Mr. Speaker. But it is there in spite of the government and not because of it. It tends to fight against the movements of the government rather than to work with this government, and the minister knows that. If she does not know it, certainly her colleagues do. Certainly the Canadian Federation of Independent Business knows it and the small businessman knows it; the army of unemployed knows it; the army on welfare knows it and those who rely on short-term government programs for short-term employment know it. They all know that the government has neglected the problems of the nation in the fields which are the subject of the motion. The minister owes this House a lot more than to come forward with that canned pap, that bit of fluff which she tried to pass off as government policy.
Let us examine the efforts the government has made on behalf of small business. The minister mentioned the throne speech, so let us see what several of them have said. On October 8, 1970, there was nothing in the throne speech about small business. On February 17, 1972, there was nothing, but then all of a sudden the government woke up. On January 4, 1973, it said there would be aid to small business with three new initiatives to strengthen management, consulting services, and to improve access to financial facilities. Nothing came of it. On February 27, 1974, the throne speech said that measures would be proposed to aid small business both financially and by providing better consulting services through the creation of a federal business development bank.
The Federal Business Development Bank has been created and the minister gave us the statistics on it. In this House we were promised that the bank would act differently than the Industrial Development Bank but we' find it is the same bureaucratic mess. It has not acted like the ordinary banking institution that the then Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce told the House it would.
On September 30, 1974, in the throne speech the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) promised to increase economic activity and give greater financial and other support to small business. Is anybody over there proud of the economic support and the increase of economic activity in this country? They must be blind if they are, and it is about time someone told them so.
In the last throne speech on October 12, 1976, the Prime Minister said that the government was going to improve local access to financial assistance and other services provided by government departments, the Federal Business Development Bank, and federal institutions to the private sector. That promise is relatively new, but like the others it has not been fulfilled.
What are the problems of small business in Canada? Just last week in its submissions to the Senate committee the Canadian Federation of Independent Business set out its goals

May 30, 1977
Small Business
as achieving low inflation, low unemployment, more balanced geographical development, a maximum feasible standard of living, a balance between owner-managed and professionally managed enterprises, and efficient use of resources.
Is anyone opposed to that, Mr. Speaker? If they are not, then the government that has to appear to move in that direction should start supporting those goals. Perhaps the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), who spoke out so violently against the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, ought to consider whether he supports those aims.
The president of the Federation of Independent Business has made a study of the problems perhaps more deeply than the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Marchand), who unfortunately cannot be here because of a personal tragedy in which we all sympathize. As reported in a press interview the Federation president, John F. Bulloch, said that current strategies were oriented toward large firms and that the complex of monetary and fiscal policy, economics of scale, specialization, rationalization, increased productivity, innovation and commercial policy under the existing socio-economic model, lumped small firms and professionally managed enterprises together.
That is one of the problems. Governments have given lip service to the problem just as they gave lip service to multicul-turalism in Canada. What did the government do with regard to multiculturalism in Canada? The government made the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz), that distinguished member of this House, minister of state for multiculturalism. The announcement was made with great fanfare. The government was to embark on a new multicultural program and pay attention to our ethnic communities the like of which they had not before experienced. Everybody said what a marvellous thing the government had done. The government accepted those plaudits; but what did it do?

The program was forgotten. And the extent of the government's neglect of multiculturalism was underscored by the appointment of the new Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Guay (St. Boniface)). What have you got against the multicultural movement in this country?

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with interest to the debate this afternoon and cannot help but feel that much said was beside the point. We recognize the contribution small business makes in Canada. In the Federation of Independent Business, in particular Mr. John Bulloch, its chairman, we have an articulate spokesman for this sector of the Canadian community. I had the opportunity of listening to Mr. Bulloch at a Liberal party conference held
Small Business
in Malton not too long ago. He made a very substantial presentation which attracted the undivided attention of those present.
In many ways I can understand the reaction of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). I regret that he is not in the chamber. That hon. member finds this kind of point of view very disturbing. It runs directly counter to the socialist dogma to which he is committed. From the small business community we hear this kind of talk about productivity. We hear the protest against paperwork. We hear the extreme desire of that group to get freedom to initiate, to conduct research and permit them to do a number of things to expand in a sector which we recognize as increasingly important.
The hon. member who just spoke, my good friend on the other side, thought the ministry of small business was a sham and would disappear. Nothing could be further from the truth. They tell us, depending on how the figures are compiled, that something like two thirds of employment and over half the payroll of this country come from small business, the expansion of the service sector, that part of the economy where people have to rely on their own efforts to produce, earn a living and get the satisfaction out of life for which they are looking. We are all aware of this.
This is an expanding sector. The government is increasingly aware of it. I am sure there will be a major contribution in the period ahead on behalf of small business, because we recognize that if we do not do something for small business in this area, we will go down the path of the United Kingdom economy. We will suffer from the "British disease". There will be a continual erosion of those things that contribute to the increasing standard of living we have come to expect.
Unlike the hon. member, my good friend who just resumed his seat, I noted a number of measures in the budget specifically designed as part of the policy for small business. I listened to the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) outline some of them, such as the credits that are available, the Federal Business Development Bank program, the expansion of loans, the measures to permit a number of small businesses to be associated in risk ventures without suffering tax penalties.
I would like to speak about one or two other measures which are in the budget. They are of particular interest to myself and some of my friends. The measure to exempt crafts from sales tax is long overdue. I have a hobby which is a matter of a great deal of interest to me. I cut and polish semi-precious stones for my own personal satisfaction. From time to time I have been associated with a very good friend who has much more talent than I will ever possess. She is a silversmith and sculptress. Occasionally when she has a problem with a stone, she comes to me. Sometimes in the periods I have not been a member of this place it has been my pleasure to work with her, trying to choose something to suit her design, purpose and cut.
She continuously complains to me about the very deadening effect of the sales tax on the craft and creativity of a group of
6070

Small Business
people associated with her. Some years ago they prepared a brief which they presented to the then Minister of Finance. When the Hon. Walter Gordon was Minister of Finance, I went to him with this problem. He said "Lloyd, I am dealing with income tax at the moment. Sales tax is another problem. I am going to get around to that. At the moment I just physically cannot do it."
We are now looking at the administration and application of the sales tax. I was particularly pleased to see this one measure which means a great deal to a group of craftsmen and craft-swomen in this country, if I may coin a phrase-I am always a little timid about how I unconsciously use "man" in the language of today. This is one contribution which will assist a number of small merchandisers.
I was particularly happy to see the total exemption proposed for those whose sales do not exceed $10,000 a year. It may be a very small item, but it is an item which exempts craftsmen and women who contribute to our quality of life. They make something in terms of their own standard of living, not usually a very generous standard of living, but the combination of the work they like to do and sufficient reward to encourage them to do it is an object of which we all approve.
I note one other matter in the budget. I can appreciate that members in the opposition did not talk about this. It attempts to do something about inflation. Anyone who has worked in the business sector and made their living from private business knows of the problem of sitting down with the accountants and seeing a profit appear at the end of a year that is not a true profit. It is an inflated profit that comes from the fact that the inventory went up in value as the general level of prices went up.
The government proposes that something like 3 per cent of the opening inventory at the beginning of the year be deductible off the top. That is a first step in recognizing that the profits that many corporations are reporting today are inflated profits. If the hon. member for Timiskaming and any member of his party were in the House, they would be thumping their desks and saying that corporation profits are far too high. They think that profit is almost a bad thing in itself. They want to increase the tax in the way their party has continually advocated.
I submit that the hon. member's party will have to face the problem of small business just like any other party in the House of Commons. This is an area where we are getting new employment, innovation and productivity increase. These are things we should never forget.
I read this motion very carefully. It talks about the failure of the government to respond effectively. I have listened carefully to the speeches that have been made thus far. We have heard about a few things that could be done which will no doubt be considered. However, in terms of a basic policy, philosophy and outline as to what we can do to assist, I submit that the government is certainly doing as much as any other government at any level in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to this debate with a great deal of interest. I commend the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) and our House leader for introducing this motion. It shows an effort on the part of this party to attempt to further the opportunities of the small business sector in Canada.
It is interesting to note that the first debate on small business in the history of Canada took place in the House of Commons on March 28. It was initiated at that time by our critic, the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley. I want to share with the House the motion moved at that time and what we put forward in the way of positive policy which we felt the government should implement with regard to the small business sector. Our motion, at that time, read as follows:
That in the opinion of this House the government should consider the advisability of implementing programs to assist the development of small business in this country, consisting of such positive initiatives as (a) allowing tax credits for investment in small business, (b) providing assistance in the formation of small business consortia, (c) changing government tender practices so that small business supplies a portion of government-purchased goods and services, (d) reducing the government paperwork burden imposed on small business.
These are areas in which the small business sector have been pushing for many years. It is interesting to note that when the president of the Canadian Association of Small Business appeared before the Senate Committee on Foreign Affairs he stated that Canada's economic future relies on the strength of its small businesses and it was time the government recognized this to be the case. I believe it is evident that the government has failed to do so. The federation's president, Mr. John Bulloch, told the committee that Canada has lagged one or two generations behind the rest of the world in aiding the development of small, owner-operated businesses. On May 26, according to an article in the Citizen, he further told the committee:
This country should have the largest small-firm sector in the world because of its geography yet Japan and Europe have far surpassed us. We do not even have a definition of what a small business is.
The article goes on:
Bulloch said developing a small business sector in Canada would mean more jobs, a more competitive economy and less reliance on the United States for imported manufactured goods. He said fostering local small businesses was particularly important in combatting regional disparities.
It is an obligation upon the government of the day to foster a climate which encourages small business. But the present
May 30, 1977

government has fostered a trend whereby the public sector has been playing a much greater role in our society. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) made a major mistake recently when he condemned the free enterprise system. The truth of the matter is that the government violated the principles of free enterprise and then blamed the system for its failure. At a time when restraint was required, the government printed more money. When economic restraint was required it bragged about the country's wellbeing and encouraged the good life. Recognition of the time lag between the performance of the U.S. and Canadian economies was not considered. Now we are paying the price for these mistakes and we face high unemployment thanks to the present government, not to the free enterprise system. Today, we need decision and action but we are faced, instead, with indecision and inertia. The government is hoping the American recovery will pull us out of our economic recession-hoping that some of their positive responses will spill over into Canada.
What we look for most is overall policy and economic guidance. All the government can do is talk about economic diversification, but it has no overall program by which this can be achieved. It has not stated its policies and does not know what the economic consequences of its actions may be.
One specific area of failure has to do with DREE grants and similar incentives. Government incentive programs of some kind are a necessity in this day and age but they should be the exception rather than the rule. How often has government provided enormous incentive funds to encourage industries to locate in particular areas, only to find the money wasted? Short term subsidies in many cases encourage economic inefficiency of the kind which arises, for instance, as a result of a lack of reasonable transportation facilities. These factors are not taken into consideration, causing subsidies to be retained on a more or less permanent basis to keep companies in operation. The effect of such government welfare programs is to increase the tax load borne by industries which are viable in themselves, thus further reducing our ability to compete in world markets.
I feel confident that we as Canadians would like to get back to the basics. I do not believe we expect something for nothing; indeed, our history has shown this to be true. What we do want from government is leadership and guidance.
Members over on the other side should have their record exposed every now and then. Consider what they have done. They have given us record inflation, record unemployment, record trade deficits, record budget deficits, record interest rates, record mortgage rates and record high prices. Also, they have contributed to a situation in which Canada is responsible for the highest level of foreign borrowing of any western nation.
So overall, the government has the worst track record in recent history, and all this without considering the revelations which have been made from time to time since I first came here, including the Sky Shops affair, various dredging scandals and so on. The government has driven our country so far into debt it is frightening. Deficit financing is not an acceptable
Small Business
way of stabilizing the economy. In the last nine years the administration opposite has come forward with eight deficit budgets out of nine. I do not understand how any government could feel proud of such a record.
What we are looking for on this side, as has been so well stated by our critic in this House, the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek), is a balanced approach to the problems of the small business sector. We should like to hear a set of economic goals; we should like to see a balanced budget without a budget deficit together with a disciplined monetary policy. An overall economic policy is required not only by the small business sector but by all sectors.
The government should consider itself fortunate, also, that the election in Quebec on November 15 turned out the way it did, because now it has an issue which it can grasp. It hopes the national unity debate will overshadow all the other issues which face Canadians today, such as the state of the economy, unemployment, inflation and the subject we are debating today.
The sad part of today's debate is that the majority of the constructive proposals put forward by my hon. friend will once again fall upon deaf ears. The economic record of the government makes many Canadians aware that unless drastic changes take place in overall economic policy we shall not have a country worth saving. As 1 say, looking at these matters in perspective it is obvious the government have the worst track record of any in recent history. 1 would hope that this government does not play with the national unity issue to the extent they will regain power, but that they will deal constructively with areas such as small business, unemployment and regional diversity.
I conclude by paying tribute to two individuals who are sitting in the gallery. They are two constituents from Pembina, a Mrs. Vicky Wirschke from Athabasca and Mrs. Pearl Baker. They have travelled several thousands of miles.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the time that I have left I would like to deal with some of the aspects in which the government program with respect to small business appears to be succeeding and some of those in respect to which it does not appear to be succeeding or at least has not yet been sufficiently developed.
Of course, we are all aware of the accomplishments which have been mentioned by some of my hon. colleagues this afternoon: the changes in the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act and the Small Businesses Loans Act. Those are matters which have already occupied the House during this session of parliament.
The changes in the budget this year were of particular importance from the viewpoint of small business. It was a very major theme in the budget address, perhaps almost the major theme. It was very much welcomed by backbenchers on this side who feel they were in large part responsible for the inclusion of those measures in the budget. One of the measures in the budget proposed a change in the treatment of employee stock options for employees of Canadian privately controlled companies, and this will give small firms a better competitive edge in being able to get good management and skilled help who might otherwise go to large corporations.
The election of tax treatment on investments will encourage more investment in high-risk ventures. The change with respect to refundable tax will encourage joint ventures between small firms. The elimination of federal sales taxes in certain areas and the provision for assistance with respect to metric conversion will also be of considerable assistance to small
May 30, 1977

business, as will the deferral of tax on voluntary sales of assets, which will make it easier for a firm to move closer to sources of supply or relocate to take advantage of a better market or to expand in newer facilities. Many of the other measures in the budget, although not directly aimed at small business, will be of great assistance to small business as well, such as the extension of the investment tax credit and the increase in the dividend tax credit. All these measures are very welcome. They are an indication of the fact that the government is very well aware of the necessity of assisting small business in Canada.
Another development which is very encouraging both as a reality and as a symbol of the recognition of the role of small business is the reduction in paper work. We have made progress in getting government departments to share information among themselves, and the changes in the Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act will exempt some 350,000 firms from at least one of their present reporting requirements by the end of 1981.
However, it has been estimated that this reduction in paper work is only about a 10 per cent reduction over-all. The change which has occurred to this point is indeed a welcome one and, indeed, in the policy paper which the minister will be presenting to the cabinet this summer, there will be further reductions planned in this area; but this is one of the places in which there is a great deal yet to be done because the burden placed on small business with respect to paper requirements is out of all proportion to the difficulty which is created for large firms. We all recognize that in order to keep adequate records of business so that the government will know where to allocate its resources it must have information, but surely there are better ways to get it than to impose many of the requirements which have been imposed upon small businesses. That, then, is one of the areas in which we would like to see further policy development.
Another area in which we would like to see further development is with respect to innovation by small corporations, and here I am indebted to the brief before a Senate committee which was presented recently by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, which has already been referred to several times. The brief has very interesting American statistics to the effect that a very large proportion of the innovations and inventions which have occurred in this century has come from individuals or from small businesses, and that even when a similar thing could be done by a large corporation, the cost to a large corporation of making the same kind of change is much greater. A small chemical company in the study which was referred to in that brief with 50 employees was able to develop a new product for $1400. A competing firm with 20,000 employees required $11,000 to accomplish the same result. I believe this is an indication of the economic value of government assistance to small businesses which can, with much fewer resources, accomplish equal and often larger results.
Of course, we are aware as well of the necessity of the availability of financing for small businesses. This is a matter which has been before the public for quite some time, but I
Small Business
think from the experience I have in my constituency office and from dealings with my constituents, it is not one which has yet been solved by the government. As long as Canadian banks and other lenders are as cautious as they are-at least in comparison with the similar institutions in our neighbour to the south-I think we will need government assistance to make sure that risk taking continues to be carried out in Canada and that those people who have good ideas and new ideas have an opportunity to develop them.
In the time remaining I would like to concentrate on one particular kind of small business because it is one which is of peculiar importance to the constituency I represent, which is an automotive constituency. We have slashed our over-all deficit with the United States under the auto pact from almost $2 billion in 1975 to $1 billion in 1976. That is a great improvement indeed. Over-all our performance under the auto pact has been extremely good. We have 11 per cent of the employment in the automotive industry in North America, although we have only 9 per cent of the market, and that is something of which we can be rightfully proud. I think no city has benefitted more from the auto pact than Windsor, but at the same time there is a down side and I submit that that is much heavier than it need be and certainly much heavier than desirable.
The deficit in auto parts continues to increase. It increased only slightly in 1976 over 1975, but the fact that it has increased is in itself an undesirable feature. It has been going up steadily. In addition, the increase in auto parts during the years the automotive trade pact has been in existence is a very large one indeed, far too large to be acceptable as a continuing feature of the auto pact. This is very relevant in the present context because the automotive assembly side, which is the side on which we are doing so well, is the domain of the large companies, the big three and to some extent their fourth competitor as well.
However, the auto parts industry is composed of many small companies, and I submit that it is very important to the future of small business in this country in general that we assist these particular small businesses in the automotive industry. I am not satisfied that the present level of financial assistance which is available under the Enterprise Development Board is as good for the automobile industry as that which existed some years back when there was a separate administration and a separate fund which operated very actively to assist companies which were involved only in the automotive business. Given the importance of this industry on the Canadian manufacturing scene and the importance of small businesses generally, it is too bad that particular form of separate assistance to small businesses in the automotive industry was dropped.
That makes it all the more important that the enterprise development board have the mandate and budget to assist small firms in the automotive business. With the kind of competition these firms face they have to be assisted in those years in which the market is not as good as they would wish it. Moreover, quite often when the market is good the sourcing of
