Small Business
auto parts, which is controlled largely by the big three in the United States; is not favourable to Canada.
Some years ago at a time when the automotive parts balance was beginning to veer toward Canada, people in my city felt that the United States government put pressure on the automotive companies in the United States-it was usually silent pressure that would be hard to establish by evidence in a court of law, but nevertheless real-to make sure that they sourced most of their products in that country. That makes it important that the Canadian government apply pressure to the automotive companies in Canada-and to the extent possible to those in the United States-to make sure that we have a fair share of the market in automotive parts. It is unfortunate that there has to be government pressure of that kind, but we cannot allow ourselves to be put in a position where pressure is being applied by only one side.
In addition, there is the necessity of a review of the auto pact. Just recently the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) said that the trade deficit on auto parts in 1976 was too big to swallow. It certainly is for my city which has suffered many of the consequences. Over all the balance is in our favour but when the balance in auto parts is against us, not only does it affect the situation of small businesses in Canada but it also affects the skilled trades, because the skilled workman plies his trade in the parts industry more than with the large companies. We are increasingly finding ourselves in the situation where, although we have large numbers of jobs, we have less and less skilled employment. That situation cannot be allowed to continue.
I would therefore strongly support the view that has been expressed in this House before that the Arthur report should be published so that all of us, especially those from automotive constituencies, can have all the latest facts with respect to the automotive trade pact, the deficit in particular. The government must adopt a vigorous position with respect to the automotive companies and the United States government in regard to the effect on small businesses in the automotive industry.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that the kind of contribution small businesses make a country is impossible to measure. It is an omnipresent contribution, but it can be indicated by the fact that when people have visited an area it is not normally the large corporations they remember but the small places that have given excellent service-the kind of service that is not always found with large corporations. That kind of character of our society which has been a very important part of our development in the last two centuries is too important not to be encouraged and given every assistance by the government.
I think my colleagues on this side of the House would wish me to say that, while we welcome the progress that has been made by the government in assisting small business, there are still some steps to be taken. We would strongly urge the government to take those steps.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEEDS OF SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to join with other hon. members in this debate on the motion before the House regarding the small business community. I want to compliment my colleague the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) not only on his motion today but also on the sincere interest he has taken in the problems of the small business community. Indeed, if it were not for members on this side of the House and for the hon. member in particular, this government would probably have forgotten altogether the small business segment of our economy. It is widely acknowledged that if it were not for members on this side continually giving attention to the problems of small businesses and pointing to the neglect of this government, a Minister of State (Small Business) would probably not have been appointed. The mere appointment of a minister is certainly not sufficient, however. What is needed and needed now are legislative measures, tax changes and incentives designed to assist this segment of our economy.
With the ever increasing rate of unemployment in this country I find it difficult to understand why this government has not recognized that the state of small businesses in Canada is an extremely vital factor in the health of our economy and of society as a whole. Nor can I understand why the government has not acknowledged the significant contribution which small businesses have made to the economy and work force of this nation.
Small business establishments are without question the very lifeline, lifeblood and backbone of our communities, our provinces and our country. They are an important segment of our economy. Small businesses, by their very nature, provide a very high degree of diversity and this diversity adds much needed stability to our communities and our country. Yet bit by bit they are slowly being phased or forced out of business.
Far too little consideration is being given to such an important group-a group which not only individually but collectively has contributed much to our economy and social well being. Small businessmen and their employees represent half the wage bill of corporations in Canada, and when you consider how many small firms are not incorporated you can see what an important segment of our economic strength we are dealing with.
I have a great deal of respect for these business people, men and women who have shown substantial managerial skills, efficiency, determination, dedication and initiative over the years that has often surpassed that shown by the leaders and management of some of our larger corporations. Many of these people who establish their own businesses over the years, unlike many larger firms today which receive billions of dollars in the form of assistance or grants from the government, received very little from their governments but built their businesses on hard work, long hours, faith in their communities, faith in themselves and faith in Canada.
Unfortunately, due to the philosophies of the present day federal government, there has been a tendency toward centralization, bigger and costlier governments, stronger and more powerful unions and larger multinational corporations. If this
May 30, 1977

trend does not reverse itself in the very near future, the free market system which built this country will continue to suffer and perhaps even eventually disappear.
Generally speaking, governments continue to consult only with large business and unions and as a result most legislation is geared to those sectors. Small businesses, which employ two-thirds of the country's work force, must thus accept laws which were not designed to deal with their problems in the first place.
No segment of society is more vulnerable to the red tape of bureaucratic power than the small and medium sized business sector. They do not have the manpower to handle the massive volume of government demands for paper work for various purposes. Too many of the small businessmen fall victim to the uncoordinated leap-frogging by government departments in their demands for more statistical information. Their productive effort is swamped by the increasing demand for completing and filling in forms and questionnaires. Laws and regulations of governments designed to regulate the activities of large corporations fail to heed small and medium sized businessmen. They often find themselves defenceless in a jungle of conflicting regulations, unless they have available the services of corporate lawyers, tax consultants and government relations men; and people of that calibre serve larger firms.
Even regulations which at first glance seem innocuous, such as the federal government's labelling act, can put many prosperous companies into financial difficulties. In this case the labelling act's requirements for products to be labelled in both official languages has led to severe problems for some small businesses, particularly importers who cannot afford to relabel many of their product lines. It is grimly ironic to these small businessmen that often as not the imported products are marketed solely in one particular linguistic region. Certainly, Mr. Speaker, the government should show a greater measure of common sense in many of these cases.
For some reason or other the government does not realize in any meaningful way that the survival of small business is inescapably linked to the survival of the mixed economy; as a result, we are now witnessing more bankruptcies in Canada than ever before. The government should be making every effort to reduce the considerable existing bureaucracy which is strangling the small business community, while at the same time providing incentive programs which by way of the tax system would be based on research and development, increased employment, productivity, export sales and expansion.
The government should also be conducting an all-out plan to reduce to the bare minimum the amount of form filling that small businesses are required to undergo. The Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Marchand) stated in an address in Maniwaki on May 19 that officials in his department calculated that the present move within the government to reduce the amount of form filling will save the small businesses, in dollar value, more than $40 million. If that admission on the part of the minister is not evidence in support of
Small Business
the case we, on my side of the House, are making, I do not know what is. I have seen no stronger evidence. If the government has used more insight in the first place before they initiated their complicated form filling program, the $40 million they are now going to save the small businessman could have bolstered various sectors of the business community in dire need of assistance, and prevented many a bankruptcy. This is just another example of the waste of taxpayers' money caused by our complex government bureaucracy.
Credit for small business enterprise creation and expansion, including that of an agricultural nature, is becoming increasingly difficult to obtain. There is a general lack of credit. I feel too many banks are turning away too many applicants. It is the government's duty to instil a more positive attitude in this regard and to promote and guarantee such loans more aggressively. I suggest as well that the incidence of inflation and greatly increased building and operating costs should lead the government to consider seriously increasing the ceiling of these much needed loans.
The government has contributed to the small businessman's appalling plight by being unable to manage the Post Office properly and establish good working relations with the postal unions. At present the working relationship is poor. Apparently the government and unions do not remember that small businessmen in Canada bear the financial brunt of lengthy and unnecessary strikes. Small business people in Canada are in the worst position to cope with this recurring situation. These strikes affect many small businessmen. When many of them are forced into bankruptcy, they must dismiss their employees. This throws those Canadians into the ranks of the unemployed, and unemployment is already at one of the highest levels Canada has ever experienced in her history. The financial losses of many small businesses, and consequent increased unemployment, loss of productivity, loss of sales, and so on, contribute further to depress an already sagging economy.
Judging from recent reports we fnay experience another costly postal strike in the near future. Despite these financial losses and despite some bankruptcies, the small businessmen generally supported the government's stand during the last postal strike. Surely such fine private and corporate citizens, our small businessmen, deserve a better break than they are presently receiving. Small business and agricultural interests are not identical, although basically similar. As I said, the average farmer is very much a businessman in his own right. For years members on this side of this House have asked the government to change the tax structure in order to create a more workable atmosphere for the agricultural community and small businesses and, more importantly, to preserve those segments of our economy.
My remarks refer particularly to the small family farm. Only in the recent budget did the government finally move in this general direction. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) is to be commended for introducing measures providing for a deferral of capital gains tax arising from the voluntary sale of land, buildings and certain other productive assets, to the extent that the proceeds are reinvested in similar assets.

May 30, 1977
Small Business
Let me say again in the House that this provision should apply to all forced sales as well. This one small provision is not enough. It will not, and should not, satisfy the needs of the small business community. We still face the grossly unfair situation whereby the farm wife or family member cannot be reimbursed for labour unless the farmer incorporates his farm. The government well knows that if this is done, if the farm is passed on to the next generation, the tax free provision is lost. It is in fact a form of blackmail designed by a government obviously bent on destroying the small family farm as a viable enterprise.
As some of my colleagues on my side of the House said earlier today, this same provision applies to small business. The government's attitude seems based on the mistaken belief that the small farm or private business enterprise, if given an equal chance, is less productive than the larger enterprise. I challenge the government to prove the truth of this with facts and figures. I submit it cannot do it. Bigger does not mean better.
The wife and family of the small businessman must suffer the same fate since, basically, the same rules apply. Salaries paid to family members cannot be deducted from income tax unless the business incorporates, thereby incurring the same disadvantages. I call on the government to end this sort of discrimination.
The Canadian Federation of Independent Business suggests, accurately, that the government's apparent theory of bigger is better is wrong. Despite the current concentration of corporate power, we are experiencing high inflation and record unemployment. Government intervention so far has proved unsuccessful; obviously, more business incentives are needed.
One of the basic problems is that everyone has income but little wealth. Too many people cannot afford even their own homes. Wealth makes possible a shift in investment, not income. There is wealth in Canadian society, but much of it is concentrated in the hands of large corporations and other large enterprises, not in the hands of individuals. I refer to individuals like average Canadian men and women who provide the foundation of our Canadian society and who day after day utilize their human resources in the face of government neglect and indifference and struggle for survival in the small business community.
There is nothing wrong with big business. Nor is there anything wrong with big profit. Indeed, both are necessary and desirable. However, we need to take steps to ensure that small business and moderate profit is not completely engulfed by the corporate giants. So far the government is failing miserably in this regard.
Incentives to small business are almost non-existent and any measures that are taken are usually of an ad hoc nature, often too little and too late, rather than part of a well organized plan designed to promote prosperous growth in the small business and agricultural communities.

Clearly, a more constructive policy is required and required now. This government has failed to provide that policy and the climate and atmosphere for the small business community to exist, to grow and, particularly, to expand. The economy of Canada has therefore suffered and Canadians have suffered. I am certain that Canadians, given the opportunity, will register their full support of this very excellent and timely motion put forth on behalf of our party by the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEEDS OF SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak today on this very important motion put forward by the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek). In view of the present economic situation in Canada, there is no matter we could speak on that would have greater importance than the small business community.
In order to have a perspective on the small business community, what it means to Canada in terms of employment and jobs and what it means in terms of adding to the economic strength in this country, it is important to point out that small business in Canada provides more than 55 per cent of all the jobs in this country. It accounts for more than 50 per cent of the dollar value of business in Canada.
Taken as an economic unit, the small business community is the single most important community in Canada. It is most important to underscore the fact that a number of nations in this world have recognized that, have yielded to the obvious and provided strata and structure in order to give incentive to small business, something Canada has not done.
Before going further, I wish to comment on some of the remarks of the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan). He stated that the most recent budget was a real thrust to small business and that the government had given an incentive to the small business community. In truth, a wide survey of small business people across this country revealed that the vast majority felt that the most recent budget did not offer small business any substantive advantage that would allow reasonable encouragement of initiative.
If we want to be very candid this evening, we have to lay out at the start that this government today has no integrated policy related to small business. There has been a ten month period absolutely void of policy since the government established a ministry in charge of small business. The Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Marchand) is still unable to define for the Canadian public what he means when talking about the small business community. That minister has not in any way put forward what might be called a small business policy.
We are lacking a number of things. The minister has not issued a policy. He has not even issued a definition of what he calls the small business community. That underscores why the minister's first trip abroad after being appointed minister was to the Soviet Union.
If we look at the international scene, we see that the United States, Japan and West Germany all have extensive policies
May 30, 1977

that are aimed at the small business community. Japan has recognized that it is the private small business community that relieves unemployment. It is important that we look at the community in Japan. It is a nation with some 110 million people. It has, by our standards today, zero unemployment. By contrast, Canada, a nation we like to think of as one of the greater nations in terms of human and natural resources, has one and a half million people looking for work. The reason we have such high unemployment in Canada today is that the government has been totally incapable of recognizing that unemployment by and large is solved by incentives given to the small business community.
There is a myth that Japan is a nation of big business producing products such as Toyotas, Datsuns, Kawasakis, Sonys, Elondas and many others. In truth, most of the people employed in Japan are associated with family and small business enterprises. That is why that nation has been able to achieve such a very high rate of employment or, by contrast, such a very low rate of unemployment.
In Canada, we have a ministry which has done little to alleviate the unemployment situation in Canada. After ten months of operation, we still have from that ministry no definition and no policy flow to give the kind of credibility to the small business community that this country thirsts for in a very longing way.
Governments are particularly susceptible to regulatory overkill. Michael J. Trebilcock, a University of Toronto law professor, revealed in his paper, "Winners and Losers in the Modern Regulatory State-Must the Consumer always lose?" that the federal government alone has created more than 100 regulatory agencies.
Last winter the Canadian Federation of Independent Business conducted 3,264 interviews amongst businessmen. It asked this question: "What is the single most important problem your business is facing today?" Heading the list: Government regulations and paperwork. As one businessman complained, "I am expected, inspected, disrespected, suspected, dejected, examined, re-examined, commanded and compelled until I provide an inexhaustible supply of money for every known need and desire or hope of the human race."
That underscores the plight that this highly regulatory government has imposed on the small business community. We have the situation well illustrated by the anti-inflation control program where the government focused on big business and organized labour. There has been a disrespect for, and a dissociation from, the small business community, from the entrepreneur, from the family life-style business that is so prevalent and so much the backbone of the Canadian fabric of our economy.
No segment of society is more vulnerable to the mechanics of bureaucratic power than the small and medium sized business sector. Carl Beigie, executive director of the C.D. Howe Research Institute, agrees that we have passed into the land of negative returns. In 1975 he wrote:
Small Business
-a proliferation in the government regulatory apparatus may have produced windfalls for the accounting and legal profession, but at the expense of the growth and efficiency of the overall economy.
Nothing could more underscore how government has imposed rules and regulations on the small business community so as to have a stifling and straitjacketing effect upon that very major and important sector of society. This is to say nothing about the tremendous social effect of over-regulation. There is an inverse relationship between individual liberty and government control.
I should like to take the opportunity this evening to read into the record a complaint I have just recently received from a constituent, Mr. Fossen from Killiam, Alberta who has a feed and farm supply operation. That business hires two people on a full time basis and during part of the season hires extra part-time help. It recently received from Statistics Canada a 14-page small print questionnaire with the demand that it be completed in 60 days or legal action would be taken. When you stopped to take a look at what that would require, by the owner of this company's own admission it would require that he shut down his business and work on his books for nothing short of 10 to 15 days. The form had such questions on it asking for the quantity of everything on hand-grain, concentrates, bran, oat flakes and so on. They wanted to know the amount of micro-mixes of all vitamins, the amount of macro pre-mixes for cattle and swine, the amount of all of the feeds they process-that is, all grain and how much of each individual one. They wanted a breakdown of all the concentrates, all the bags, all the electricity used, all the gas, all the office supplies, all materials used in production, equipment used by own labour force, and purchases of all goods from other sources for resale in same condition as purchased. They wanted a list of all complete foods purchased and sold, all reserves of animal and pet feeds, whether for birds, rabbits, dogs. The list goes on for 14 pages. This is an example of the way in which regulations are imposed on small business which does not have the wherewithal or the capital to be in a position to respond.
The owner of this small plant said that had the request come at a time of the year when he normally did his yearly inventory it would not have been difficult to have complied because the information had to be assembled for tax purposes anyway. But this insensitive government is now, twice a year, imposing such requirements as these on small business simply because one department or another decides it needs information. I submit that this is the kind of attitude which is endangering the small business community to the extent that it may wind up as an extinct species.
Now let me take a look at metric conversion. I am not opposed to it in principle but certainly this program has been put forward without any consultation with the farm community. Anyone who was a representative of a farm community would have known that three prairie provinces produce the bulk of the grain in this country. There is a road grid across Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta one mile east to west by

May 30, 1977
Small Business
two miles north to south. The grid is divided equally, then, into acres. The hectare will simply not fit in with the units which are already there. The government has not suggested the prairies be resurveyed. Obviously the farmers were not consulted before these changes were made.
We have read in the propaganda put out by the government that 95 per cent of the world lives on the metric system. What the government does not recognize is that there is no pure metric system which exists throughout the world. There is the Japanese metric system with all its differences relevant to Japan. There is the German metric system with its own differences relevant to Germany. There are the metric systems of almost all the countries in the world with their exceptions. But somehow the government felt they needed to take it in its pure form and impose it on Canada irrespective of the damage it might do to some sections of society. If there is to be any real feeling for the Canadian people there has to be a reversal of attention in terms of how we employ the concept of the hectare and the kilometre as opposed to the acre and the mile.
I turn now to another point. I was very pleased that the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) brought it up earlier today because I think it is an important one. I refer to the way we treat the family unit in small business today. I speak particularly of the husband and wife combination. Coming, as I do, from a farming constituency, I know what an insult it is when we witness the farm wife for a very large part of a year in a good many families working like a hired man, side by side with her husband, operating farm equipment, tending the cattle and other livestock, lifting heavy loads and then in the spring of the year being written off as a tax deduction for $1,418. What an insult it must be when those are her wages-simply a tax deduction. She knows her husband cannot pay her a salary because, if he does, she is taxable on that salary too. He also knows that he cannot do it unless he incorporates as a family business.
Incorporation for many farmers is not a practical alternative. We are in a situation today when that farmer can go out and hire a hired man to help him and write the hired man's expenses off as a tax deduction. When his own wife helps him, all he can do is write her off as a tax deduction. I think that is a scandal, not only in the farming community but in any small business such as a corner grocery store when two partners work side by side. Greater attention has to be given to this kind of system so that the entrepreneur who has initiative, ambition and the inspiration to get ahead is able to have incentive provided by government.
What we are witnessing today is the focus of government on the two major forces I mentioned earlier, big business and organized labour. No attention is paid to one really important sector of our society, the small business community. It has been demonstrated around the world that countries which have been able to keep a buoyant economy have provided incentives for small family businesses.
While talking about the small business community I should like to deal for a moment or two with the subject of labelling and how the present requirements act as a disincentive to the
(Mr. Malone.]
small entrepreneur for many reasons. The labelling legislation makes a lot of sense in terms of business which is conducted nationally. But consider the fact that some of the finest western boots made in Canada are made in Quebec, or that some of the best kayak paddles obtainable in this country are made in Quebec. Here is an example of where the labelling legislation might well apply. It applies equally in other areas of production such as the canneries at Lethbridge which see their products across Canada. But it does not apply to those industries either in English Saskatchewan or in French Quebec which are totally local. In these circumstances, to have to comply with the labelling regulations means another capital investment simply to get their ideas on the market.
One of the things that should not happen in Canada is that you have to pay an extra price in order to take some initiative. If you want people to have incentive, you ought to reward people for that, rather than pile up the bureaucratic overkill of paperwork which is imposed upon small businesses by the rigid, over-regulating government which we have at the present time. There are many small businesses which would very much appreciate an opportunity to get out from underneath all of the paperwork which is presently imposed upon them. Small business has a very different set of needs from the multinational organizations. We do need tariffs for protection from the giant textile industries, but they need not apply to the small speciality shops.
In my own constituency there is a store which sells only western shirts and clothing. By the laws of Canada, that store cannot buy any tariff-free shirts except from eastern Canada; it cannot buy western shirts because they do not make them. They have to compete with their neighbours down the street who can buy the tariff-free goods. On the other hand, we find the people who are importing these shirts getting them from the western United States and from other countries who are making western clothing. They have to pay tariff on them, and that acts as a disincentive to them.
The survival of the broadbased middle class is vital to democracy. Likewise, the small business community is an integral part of the economic mix of this country. However, securing risk capital at the present rate of loan interest in Canada makes a good idea too expensive. In the final analysis, Canada as a nation has to be the loser.

speechtext:
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I would also like to thank my colleagues and friends in the House for giving me an extension of time. Before concluding, I have a few more comments to make.
May 30, 1977

Even after a decade of rapid inflation, the ceiling on small business loans of $50,000 should be readjusted upwards so as to account for the inflationary trends of this past decade. If we are going to have a situation where small business entrepreneurs can establish themselves, get their feet on the ground and offer viable alternatives in Canada for employment, then we have to think of businesses capitalizing themselves somewhat in excess of a rate of $50,000. Presently the government's approach to unemployment is to give the people of Canada make work programs through such concepts as LIP, LEAP, Young Canada Works and Canada Works. If the state has no business in the nation's bedrooms, then it has no business frustrating the basement offices of its homes either.
The government is hoping that by some kind of make work programs it can solve unemployment. All that it does with its make work programs is to shift from make work during one half of the season to unemployed people during the other half of the season. In other words, in Canada today we have a coin which has on one side heads-make work-and on the other side tails-unemployment. Either way Canada is losing, because on that kind of a flip of a coin you cannot come out a winner.
If we had more incentive for the small business community, we would have ongoing employment such as would match West Germany, Japan and the United States. All three of those countries have specialized departments and incentives to give encouragement to small business groups. There should be a tax credit incentive for small businesses which would do more for free enterprise than the current focus on organized labour and the multinationals. It would do more for free enterprise than would all the make work programs this government can dream of. Make work programs are merely an extension of unemployment, except with a stop gap. It is a band-aid which does not cure the ailment but simply hides it and puts it away.
I will conclude by saying that the small and medium-sized businesses, managed by the small or medium-sized operations, hire 60 per cent of Canada's labour force. That is a fact we have to address ourselves to, and that is a fact which the Japanese, the West Germans and the Americans have addressed themselves to. Their economies reflect their governments' sensitivities to the needs of their people. I hope this government will see fit to adopt the motion being put forward here today.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEEDS OF SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very grateful to have an opportunity to speak today. It is only seven months ago that I left the business world, and I feel I still have a strong sense of what should happen to small business.
It was in December 1971 that F. H. McNeil, President of the Canadian Bankers' Association said:
Confidence is low among Canadian businessmen because they believe many government attitudes and policies are either irrelevant or fundamentally detrimental to Canada's interests . . . Businessmen are frustrated and disenchanted.
Small Business
The federal government, if it is interested in small business, must either play a role in providing the financial capital required for expansion or legislate changes in the Bank Act to provide the incentive to the financial community to generate a larger proportion of the monetary needs of small business.
However, there is a need for more money. Managerial talent and organizational restructuring are also very important and key to the life and survival of small business. Government could increase support to the provinces to improve the quality of education in business schools, MBA programs and the wonderful programs which are happening in community colleges.
The situation facing Canada today is critical. The problems of small businesses do not only mean an increase in bankruptcies and resulting unemployment, which is serious enough on its own, but by failing to support and basically hindering small business in Canada, the federal government is denying an important resource to our struggling economy.
The catalogue of difficulties facing small businesses in Canada is complex and lengthy. I would like to explore some of them now. One problem which many small businesses have to cope with is the enormous volume of red tape existing in Canada today. A study by the Law Reform Commission reported in 1975 that federal statutes have now created some 20,000 criminal or quasi-criminal offences. Provincial statutes account for another 20,000 such laws. This has meant an ongoing transfer of decision-making powers and economic resources from the private sector to the state. The situation led to complaints such as "governments are increasingly hostile to business" and "the bureaucracies are apparently anti-business".
I am afraid the worst problem is here in Ottawa, because it has become so remote, because it is so vague and because it appears inbred. In some of our large public service emporia they are only interested in talking to people who come from equal size broadloomed offices. Small business must have consultation with all levels of organization, especially with senior officials and ministers who are out of touch with small business.
I recommend the story of an Ontario cabinet minister who, in the last two years, has taken two Winnebagos and travelled the length and breadth of Ontario to talk to tourist industry owners right in their own homes and travel agencies. What has happened is that Ontario has begun to design the right kind of incentives and programs for the travel industry.
Another problem for small businesses is in the area of government tenders. There is a need for change in government tender practices so that small business supplies a portion of government purchased goods and services. As has been stated here earlier today, Canada lacks a small business act. Under small business legislation in the United States, however, one third of federal spending for goods and services goes to small business. Imagine a third of all purchases of our federal

May 30, 1977
Small Business
government going to the small business community. What a lift that would make!
In 1950 cash spent by governments amounted to 28 per cent of our national income; now it is 46 per cent and rising. In order to collect this money, the government has evolved an intricate tax philosophy and tax policy. The whole area of taxation is another government induced problem faced by small business. The corporate rip-off in Canada is that half of our profits are going to governments which put in little capital, man hours, or risk in order to benefit from business. It is not uncommon, for example, for governments to encourage business through tax allowances. The businessman then risks his capital, time and in many cases forgoes income for a number of years-at which time government calls the tax allowances "loopholes" and closes the tax gap. Where have we heard that before?
Any new venture requires planning, research and development, financing, staffing, the construction of production facilities and marketing. Even in a successful program, there is a long waiting period between the initial outlay and a return on capital. Any change in a tax law without notice is unfair; such changes are now being complicated by retroactive tax laws.
Taxation should be designed not to produce revenue but as a device to influence the economy. Governments frequently tax at the wrong time, at the wrong place and in order to gain immediate funds. The Canadian economy is often compared to a pie, and we argue about how the pie should be divided. Forgive me if I bring a note about the bakery industry into my speech. We argue about how the pie should be divided. Instead, we should worry about first making the pie. The major ingredient in this kind of baking is real wealth, and our taxation system should aim at increasing it.
The Canadian taxation system should work to motivate people to greater production. Our taxation system is now frequently aimed at punishment when it should encourage productivity and efficiency. Government should attempt to keep taxation simple and the cost of collection at a minimum. That Chinese expression "Do not remove a fly from your friend's head with a hatchet" is a motto which I believe our taxation department officials should have on their wall.
Decision-making in business is now being turned from factors of economic efficiency to considerations of taxation. The best efforts of many small businesses are now towards bending the best principles of sound business practice to fit an unsound taxation policy. Our incredibly intricate and therefore expensive collection system, coupled with a high rate of taxation, is producing disastrous side effects and undesirable changes in our economy for which our citizens never voted.
So that you do not think I am just being negative or critical, let me point out that our party has proposed some sound changes. One of the more recent comprehensive statements on taxation came from the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), in his reply to the March 31 budget on April 4, 1977. He proposed a tax credit for small businessmen investing in research and development. As the small business sector is already one of the most innovative groups in the Canadian

economy, these efforts to advance the technological capability of this country should be rewarded. The Progressive Conservative proposal would form an alliance between the goals of increased research and development, a reduction in regional disparities and the encouragement of small business-a fortunate coincidence of goals.
Under the proposal, a small businessman could obtain a tax credit for investment in research and development. The credit would be on a sliding scale, depending upon whether the project was taking place in an area of regional disparity. The amount of the rebate could range from a high of, say, 75 per cent in the Atlantic region and Quebec to a low of 25 per cent or less in the more prosperous areas of the country. A substantial proportion of the tax revenue lost by such a credit would be regained as a result of the new employment opportunities created. Such investments in R & D will result in increased economic growth over the long-term and a more stable basis for the Canadian economy.
Another proposal is for long-term fiscal or tax contracts for companies investing in areas of regional disparity. This proposal would be of particular benefit to the medium sized owner-managed company which would be willing to take the risk of investing in a slow growth area. The purpose of the tax contract would be to provide some degree of tax certainty for a company willing to undergo the financial uncertainty of investment in an area of regional disparity.
The sort of contract our party is thinking of would be of the following kind. A company thinking of investing in, for example, Newfoundland would sign an agreement exempting the operations of the new investment until, say, 150 per cent of the investment had been recovered or until ten years, after the plant begins production. Both of these tax proposals are designed to assist both in fostering the small business sector and reducing regional disparities. They are grouped together because the goals of a strong small business sector and of regional development are complementary-in fact, they are so complementary as to be mutually necessary.
Several unfortunate experiences in the past, such as the Shaheen Come-by-Chance Refinery, Bricklin, etc., should show us that big business may not be the answer to regional development. You cannot build an adequate, large scale industrial infrastructure from scratch. Without infrastructure, large scale industry cannot survive. Without large scale industry, there is no need for an industrial infrastructure. Further, because small business is more labour intensive than capital or energy intensive, a predominantly small business economy in areas of regional disparity will escape many of the problems associated with high energy and transportation costs. Small and medium sized firms are far more likely to make permanent contributions to regional development than are world scale plants, and that will be a benefit conferred by our proposals for small and medium sized business.
Another positive suggestion is that small business feels the weight of government regulation and paperwork far more than larger companies which can afford the armies of lawyers and accountants required for compliance. This administration has
May 30, 1977

announced its intention of reducing the burden of regulation upon business. There is even some scant evidence that an effort is being made to reduce the paperwork burden. But in the meantime, government imposes costs upon business-costs which fall most heavily upon the owner managed sector.
Our party has proposed that there be a tax rebate for small businessmen who must cope with federal government paperwork. The rebate would only be a token amount in terms of the costs imposed, but it would involve a financial recognition of the costs the public bureaucracy imposes upon small firms, and, more importantly, it would provide a financial incentive for the federal government to reduce its paperwork.
Another point is investment incentive credit. All Canadians should be encouraged to invest in small and medium sized business. Larger corporations can afford to pay interest on bonds or dividends on equity. Those who purchase these instruments can take advantage of an interest income deduction or a dividend tax credit. No such treatment is available to investors in a small business, simply because the average small business is in no position to sell stocks or issue bonds. Anyone who has seen what is required for that kind of thing knows that small business cannot handle it. A small businessman gets his money from his own resources, his friends, his neighbours, local lawyers, doctors or often from his mother-in-law, but those creditors may not get their money back for years, if at all. Why should these people who invest in Canada's future- not people who buy stocks or bonds-not get a tax break as well? Our party suggests that they should and that at the very least the investor in a small business should get the same tax break as an investor in a large corporation.
Since 1972 our party has pressed for an investment credit scheme. An investment credit should be available to any Canadian citizen who makes a direct investment in the equity of a Canadian owned, small owner-managed business. The credit, which could amount to 50 per cent of the value of a qualified investment up to a maximum of $5,000 per year, should either be offset against an individual's income tax for the year or rebated directly to him. Qualifying investments should include direct participation in proprietorship or partnership as well as investment in the new equity offerings of medium sized corporations. 1 cannot help but feel that this last proposal would have a profound effect on small businesses, especially in the outlying areas of the country.
If the small businessman had unlimited funds, there would be fewer tax problems for him to worry about. He could indulge in investment in multiple corporations, offshore vehicles, sophisticated annuities and capital reorganizations. He could set aside days to confer with tax assessors, supervisors, and valuators of Revenue Canada, locally and in Ottawa, only to find that simple solutions are no longer available.
The small businessman or woman fights survival in an age of technocracy where the majority of politicians do not comprehend the complexity of the laws they pass. Today if you enter into any unusual business deal without advice, you are
Small Business
often in very heavy tax trouble. Getting advice brings the realization that a person involved with small business must have lawyers, C.A.'s and insurance people who specialize in tax laws and that the general practitioner in these fields can no longer provide all the answers. The small businessman finds that soaring professional costs, because of the increased time which now must be spent on these things, have no return.
Above all, the small businessman finds uncertainty. He is asked to make certain decisions with regard to his future and that of his family, to reorganize, to pay out fees, and pay out thousands of dollars for insurance, valuations and trust companies, all essentially costly and nonproductive. He has no guarantee that solutions will work, that the government will agree or that laws mean what they seem to mean, let alone that laws will not radically change in future years.
It is far easier in tax planning for him to remain with as simple a structure as possible and to sacrifice tomorrow's future tax advantage for today's uncertainty. So he puts off adding that addition to the factory. He puts off buying that piece of equipment which would employ four or five more people. He decides it is just too complicated, and his business stays the size it is. A company which is not dreaming and growing begins to fall back, and hon. members know the end of that story.
In spite of the fact that a number of brilliant specialists, in government and in the professions, revel in their ability to think of long words and legalese, the majority of tax advisers as well as Revenue Canada and the Department of Finance would prefer a simpler and more comprehensible law. The entire act should be rewritten so that it can be comprehended by the taxpayer. I am afraid that the laws today are framed in ambiguity and absurdity, which will continue to confound both judges and practitioners until corrected.
From the point of view of small business the administration of tax laws has become as critical as the laws themselves. Solutions have been suggested continually by the joint Bar-CICA taxation committee and organizations of business, but there seems to be no outward indication that the problems are being dealt with. Instead of leadership, I am afraid we have musical chairs. We have had Mr. Benson, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien), Mr. Cote, the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), the hon. member for York-Sear borough (Mr. Stanbury), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Basford), and the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen); and now, with all due respect, perhaps it will be different because we have a lady, the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin).
Whether the problems are philosophical or whether there are problems in communications, lack of policy is critical at this point. I only hope that the government will begin to see that two things are needed. The first is a change of attitude within the tax department, and the second is an over-all long range policy for small business.

speechtext:
Hear, hear!

May 30, 1977
Small Business

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEEDS OF SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
I am going to end on a hopeful note. In April, just a month or two ago, the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Marchand) spoke to the western regional newspapers' annual meeting at Banff, and in that speech he said:
I intend to do what I can to get government off the backs of small entrepreneurs, so that they can get on with running their businesses and making a profit. Profit is not a dirty word with the federal government, and small business is too important not to get a fair shake and a fair share from Ottawa.
Those are wonderful words. I urge the minister and his colleagues to make that statement a reality.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEEDS OF SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the debate from the very beginning today on this peculiarly opportune motion by the opposition relating to small business, and I do not think any person listening and wondering as I have been today would hesitate in saying that the latter part of the remarks of the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott) put the finger on the solutions more succinctly and aptly than any other speeches made today.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEEDS OF SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEEDS OF SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
One of the
weakest parts of the policy making of all parties in this House for 30 years has been in the field of small business, and this motion today, which focuses on this question, does a great service. There is no question that despite the federal government and all the provincial governments this is still primarily a private enterprise country. Over 50 per cent of the labour force of this country works for incorporated small businesses, and an additional percentage-the figure we never know for sure- works for unincorporated small businesses. We have that amount of the labour force working in incorporated or unincorporated small businesses-it is well over half-and we have this combination of inflation and unemployment which the economists do not know how to resolve because, according to them, it has never happened before.
The economists know nothing about history. The only thing they ever learn is what they are told by their economics professors at university. They think all wisdom came from Adam Smith, Ricardo and perhaps Keynes and, if they are "with it", from Galbraith. The fact is that economists do not know the first thing about the problems of inflation and unemployment when they arise at the same time. These subjects are so important that we cannot leave them to these people who look at the world through a long pipe.
It is obvious that the government is willing to help small business, but it is equally obvious that the government does not know how to do it. The answer, which I think was suggested better than anybody else by the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton, is that taxation is the key. Our taxation system is based on the philosophy that you have to be big to be good and that the only thing that works is economy of scale. That is what it says in the economics textbook.
The agricultural field is a small business field where literally 95 per cent of the operations are owner managed. The greatest growth in Canada since the war has been in the field of

agriculture. Whereas growth across the country has averaged 2'k to 3 per cent, agriculture has maintained a growth rate of over 7 per cent.
The government under Mr. Pearson collected all the brains in the economic field from government, universities and private business, and all agreed that in Canada there were three times too many farmers and that the way to get efficiency was to reduce the number to one-third. All these economists agreed there was too much land in production and that the thing to do was to reduce the productive land in the prairies, the great agricultural area of Canada, to half. That was true not only in connection with farms. They had the same attitude toward small business-that there were too many of them and that we should have big business.
Every speaker on this side of the House today has brought into his remarks the characteristic of government tax law- that everything is in favour of largeness. In the case of agriculture we have the Vulcan study in Alberta and the Ontario government's study on agriculture which demonstrate beyond any argument that productivity comes at its maximum in these owner-controlled enterprises with two pairs of hands. A man and his wife, a man and his son, a man and his daughter or a man and his hired man, give the highest level of unit productivity. Because the ownership and the management of our farms are usually under one person, we have attained a growth rate in productivity of 7 per cent per year for 30 years when all other business has only averaged 2Vi or 3 per cent. We have the studies to prove this in agriculture, but of course the government does not read such studies.
This government accepts the doctrine of the economists that business has to be big, so the tax law reveals how to get exemptions by adding to cost. The more people you employ, they say, the more you can deduct from income; the more expenses you incur, the more you deduct. As a result, as the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Pigott) pointed out the small businessman cannot compete because he cannot hire the accountants, tax advisers and all the other people to figure out ways to use the complicated tax laws to add to the expenses of the company so that it pays less tax. Therefore, the businessman, ipso facto, is discriminated against in the tax burden.
Now I want to say something on the positive side as well, Mr. Speaker. It is not only in agriculture or in the small business enterprise that you get innovation and productivity. Let us examine so-called big industry-the oil and gas industry. We have all heard of Imperial Oil; it is a little subsidiary of Exxon. It gets the credit for discovering Leduc in Alberta in 1947. It was not the big brains of Exxon or Imperial that discovered oil at Leduc. One lonely geologist for years fought the big boys at the top who all believed the same textbook and were wrong. He pleaded with them to look at the reef structures beneath the surface in Alberta. Because this was the last well of all, the companies that had been drilling unsuccessfully in Alberta for 20 years, as a kindness to one of their junior
May 30, 1977

geologists, agreed to put a pipe on the reef field. That was the beginning of the discovery of the 50 billion barrels of oil that have fuelled Canada since. That happened because of one individual, a man who could think and who had the vision you must have to make changes. I think our whole oil and gas industry should be a monument to this man. His name is not known. Even the president of Imperial Oil, Mr. Twaites, who retired two years ago did not know about it. This man's name is forgotten except by old timers in the industry.
Now let us look at farm machinery. We have big companies that produce machinery worldwide. How many of the new improvements put on the cultivators, the ploughs, the combines, the seeders come from the big companies? Almost invariably they come from a farmer who has figured out the answer to a problem. The farmer designs the hydraulic system that makes each of his cultivator teeth stay at the same depth in the soil regardless how hard it is. Individual farmers have figured out the answer to their problems. Usually a local manufacturer tries to produce the item that makes the implement work better. Only then do the big companies come in to buy up the idea and incorporate it in their machinery.
I could go through almost all the types of things used in the productive machinery of the large corporations in the resource field across this country, whether it be mining, oil and gas, farming or the forest industry. Almost invariably it is the man who has to grapple with the problem of handling the big tree on the side of the hill who figures out how to do it. They call these people "hay wire farmers" but these are the men who are giving Canada productivity in the forest industry, the agricultural industry, the mining industry and the oil and gas industry. These are the men who develop machines to crawl across the muskeg. They are not from some foreign country but are Canadians and, I might say, most are from the farm.
This is our genius-the ability to adapt; this is our genius- the ability to work out a solution, both practical and economic. We do not have to back down one step to any nation in the world in translating fundamental scientific and engineering ideas into practical, workable machinery. Our scientists and engineers have not let us down, but there is a tremendous gap between what they do and what scientists and engineers at the government level and at universities do because we have not got the means to translate that into applied operations. Usually it is a farmer or a man working close to nature in the forest or mine who finds out something about these theories-and sometimes even without finding out, produces a new idea.
I should like to wind up my remarks with a few words about opportunity, Mr. Speaker. Never has Canada had a greater opportunity in the area of small business than today. I am not talking about the merchandising field which has been well covered today; I am talking about the small entrepreneur who produces new ideas. It is obvious that over the next 30 years we have to shift from our practice of producing raw materials without consideration for recycling or using renewable forms of raw materials. It is in this field that Canada leads the world.
If we look around to see who has done most to make it possible for us to shift smoothly to cheaper ways of producing
Small Business
heat and energy, we find Canada is in the lead. We owe this to our universities, the National Research Council and the practical people in the field.
A good example is the National Research Council. In Ottawa it developed a vertical windmill that runs silently. All you have to do is put an induction motor on the bottom and plug it into any outlet which will turn those two blades. Because it is in motion, a wind at two miles an hour will reverse that induction motor into a generator. This cheap little $60 motor that you could take off the bottom of your washing machine will transform that two-mile per hour wind into one of 12 miles per hour, giving three or four times more power than your house would need. Obviously it will not work when there is no wind. It produces more power than you need when there is wind but when there is no wind it does not produce enough power.
Who would be better able to produce this than the small Canadian businessman? Yet there are only two Canadian firms producing this windmill because most are only interested in producing large windmills costing $1 million or $2 million that the government will buy. The farmer, or person living on the windy hilltop or beside the lake is interested in buying one for about $3,000 with which to produce power for his home or farm. He can sell the surplus back to Ontario Hydro, Saskatchewan Hydro, B.C. Hydro, or even the Hydro Commission in Nova Scotia. Farmers understand this, because 40 years ago they all used windmills. When hydro came along and gave the farmers an alternative to the noisy, straight line propeller-driven windmills, people in rural communities began using hydro power. On windy days farmers could sell their surplus power to hydro. If the wind dropped, hydro could turn on one of its water generating plants to provide power until such time as the wind picked up again. In this way, hydro could stand by with extra generating facilities for a calm day.
This proposal could apply to between 50 per cent and 60 per cent of all Canada. I could apply to much of Quebec, parts of Ontario, certainly those communities next to lakes and rivers, and to all of the west. In the west we have more wind then you can shake a stick at. This sort of power could be cheaper than conventionally generated power, but big business will not build the facilities. It is interested in selling the machinery it is already producing.
What programs are there in Canada for encouraging small business to become involved in this enterprise? The design work has been done and prototypes of the equipment are in place. One piece of equipment has been running for years on top of the National Research Council building. Another piece has been operating for the last two years a mile or so west of Regina. The demonstration period is over. The equipment has been brought back to Ottawa. Why can we not institute a positive policy whereby Canadian business will be encouraged to produce such equipment? It is simple to reproduce. Let us make it available to the half million, or even two million homes and farmers who could use it in this country-I am not sure

May 30, 1977
Small Business
what the number is. But you can only do it if you accept the sort of proposal the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mrs. Piggott) made, namely give to small business some of the advantages you give to big business. Let us give small business a tax write-off. Let us give them some power of leverage, which involves part of the cost of equity and part of the cost of financing. Mr. Speaker, we lend farmers hundreds of millions of dollars and lose nothing. Farm credit is amazing. No business can meet the credit rating of a farmer on repayment. The same would hold true with regard to power generating equipment.
Second, I raise another farm-related subject, methane production. People have been producing methane for lighting and heating their homes for 6,000 years. Methane is produced mainly in warm countries. Why can we not produce it in a cold country? It is produced in universities, but I have seen only one farmer using it full time. Why cannot we encourage methane production, especially on the farm? If a farmer can raise hogs or cattle and thereby make $10,000 a year, I suggest he could make $20,000 profit with the methane produced from those animals. If he removes the methane from the animal waste, he can increase the value of its fertilizer component fourfold.
Since one ordinary herd in western Canada could produce enough methane to heat four homes, I should think the government should consider giving tax advantages to encourage methane production. They can produce methane in universities, and methane is used in a project in southern Manitoba. Of course, someone has to keep track of costs. A farmer must know what it costs him to produce methane. He, himself, will need to do much of the work, because help on the farm is hard to come by. I would think it would be a good idea to give some incentive for the production of methane.
As well, we could use the protein content of waste material. I read an article the other day saying that 21 cities in the United States are using their garbage to make money. If we could only use the protein contained in animal waste on North American farms, my God, we could generate hundreds of millions of dollars of income. The figures are in the scientific records, and they show that one ton of cow manure-if I may mention it in this august place-is worth about $3 if it is just dumped on the land. If you take the methane out, you increase its value as fertilizer-and have the benefit of the use of the methane-to $30 a ton. That same ton of manure, if it is recycled by chemical means and turned into absolutely pure cattle food meeting all the standards of the FDA, the Canadian Department of Agriculture, is worth about $140 a ton. Mr. Speaker, such enterprises ought to be under way in Canada in 500 places, and all could be making a profit. All should be paying tax on that profit. And only small business can do it, because only small business people can handle, say, the 50 tons of manure a day involved in the operation.
I tell the House all this to show that private enterprise is not dead. Private enterprise has a tremendous future. If the government thinks private enterprise consists only of very large firms and tailors our tax laws to suit these enterprises, that

future cannot be ours. The men who guide the destinies of this government and believe that bigger is better on the farm, better in industry and better in merchandising are dead wrong. I believe the task force report of 1969 was dead wrong. I believe the report was monstrous and did an injustice not only to the producers of Canada but to those who want the food they produce. Yet we are ruled by a government dedicated to the proposition that we must reduce the number of farmers, and get rid of small businessmen and small farmers to boot. I say without hesitation that we are right to criticize the government for not acting as quickly as possible on the question of small business.

speakeroldname: Hon. Marcel Lessard (Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-NEEDS OF SMALL BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the remaining few minutes, I would like to comment this evening on some statements that were made today. I have had of course an opportunity to look at what was said by some members here about the federal government's small business policy. Of course they enjoyed referring to what should have been done rather than what has been done. It is quite normal that the opposition criticize the government, especially of course on allotted days.
But if we examine the subject of today's debate and the wording of the non-confidence motion, I suggest we find little there of real substance. The hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek), who was responsible for today's debate, did not deem fit to remain very long in this House to hear what his colleagues had to say, or what other opposition members would add to his remarks. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that he did not put forward proposals that could bring any change for the small business community.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to differentiate as far as small businesses are concerned. There are two kinds of firms in my view: Those that produce goods as such, and they alone add real value. On the other hand, there are firms that deal in trade as such, and they also are headed by businessmen. The latter of course are needed, and I recognize the value of their services to the community, but there is a basic difference in that they add no value as such to the goods they handle. They add to the cost, of course, because their services in warehousing and merchandizing goods made by the other sector, the manufacturing sector, entails costs, and those costs are passed on to the consumer.
Admittedly, their services are needed. But there is a difference, Mr. Speaker, because what is adding actual value to the goods is the small processing, manufacturing industry in Canada. That is the one we must help the most. Of course, we need the one that is active in the commercial aspect of business, but it can easily take off and prosper when the market and the demand exist, when the consumers exist and they have the money to spend; but, with production, the matter is much more complex, Mr. Speaker, because it requires initiatives; the risks are greater, it takes more capital and
May 30, 1977

technological know-how. And that is not easily found everywhere.
That is why the government must, through its policy, preferably encourage those people who are in the manufacturing and processing industry. That is why we have a plethora of government measures, under the Departments of Industry, Trade and Commerce, of Finance, and ours, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, and also the new one entrusted to the hon. member for Kamploops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand), Minister of State for Small Business. Those are four government departments which help small businesses specially, among other responsibilities, of course.
Take the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, for instance: 80 per cent of all companies we help are small manufacturing or processing industries, which get financial assistance either through direct grants or loans, or loan guarantees to help them start out in business, to expand or even modernize their operations. The government has several programs. There is the technological research program, which provides various forms of help from the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. When I hear hon. members of the opposition say those are not good enough, I would appreciate their being much more specific about what new forms of assistance there could be. They talk of help through tax exemptions: we have had, for years, what is known as investment tax credit.
Small businesses, large businesses and even farms are eligible for tax exemption, assistance plan or tax credit which is available to help them in their investments. I cannot understand how members of the opposition can stand up in the House and state categorically that the federal government does not help small business. We also consult small businessmen, we have consultations and meetings with them, and they tell us what they need, what is wrong with the present system, what they would like to see changed in our laws and regulations. For instance they told us that they would like to see better consistency between the various programs of the government, a reduction in the number of forms and reports they have to fill in, and we are doing that now, because it meets their needs. We have made funds available to them.
There is the Small Businesses Loans Act, research is available to them, there is also assistance to prospection for foreign markets, one federal agency gives them credit guarantees and export credits. Here in Ottawa, we have devised a variety of schemes offered to all businesses, small, medium or large, to help them do business and I cannot see why it should be necessary to add any others as it has been suggested. Our economic system is going through a difficult time. The demand is not as strong as one would hope, because in Canada during the last few years, due to a feeling of uncertainty, people have chosen to save more, and reports that we regularly receive each month indicate that Canadian savings are highest ever.
Adjournment Debate
One can therefore predict, Mr. Speaker, that with the return of a certain degree of confidence within the public at large, purchases will increase, the general demand will grow and manufacturing businesses will regain those customers they had lost, and this will necessarily put them in a position to make greater profits.
One could elaborate on this, Mr. Speaker, but I would rather say a word about what our department has been doing lately particularly towards helping small businesses. We had been told that there were a lot of talented people in certain areas, numerous individuals with no lack of initiative who had excellent projects which they could not launch because they did not have the necessary funds with which to get those small units started. During the past few months our department started a special experimental program designed to assist the kinds of entrepreneurs who did not have the wherewithal to get their small businesses off the ground. We have offered them direct subsidies, additional financing and some technical assistance. This program seems to be making a headway and encountering a lot of success particularly in New Brunswick where it has literally been extended to all that province. Mr. Speaker, within the coming months I am definitely planning on trying this program in other parts of Canada, in other provinces, because this is a way of helping those small entrepreneurs rich in ideas and creativity who have been able to determine certain needs in the market and who have a keen feeling for innovation, mainly in order that they be able to create new products, new types of goods which will answer the needs of consumers, be they Canadian or foreign consumers likely to import their products.
I would like to conclude by saying that the government is well aware of the need of small businesses for constant support. We are ready to consider any serious and substantial suggestion likely to help small businesses, but it is certainly not during a debate of this type, it is surely not by reading the speeches made in this House that small businesses will feel reassured because even though the speeches made today contain many ideas, they contain even more contradictions. I do not think that this is the way to reassure small businesses.
Mr. Speaker, I see that your patience is at an end. I shall not abuse it any longer except to say that the opposition did not necessarily gain anything today by attacking the small businesses assistance policy of the government. I believe that results speak for themselves. The government has the support of small businesses and small businessmen and this is why it will long continue to have the confidence of Canadians.

subtopic: AIRPORTS-MIRABEL AND DORVAL-REASON REVENUE NOT RECEIVED FROM HOST RENT-A-CAR
AIRPORTS-MIRABEL AND DORVAL-REASON REVENUE NOT RECEIVED FROM HOST RENT-A-CAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 24 in reply to a question I directed to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) he confirmed in his own indirect way that his department was not receiving revenues on a monthly basis from Host Rent-a-Car at the Quebec City, Dorval and Mirabel airports due to the fact that Host, to quote the minister, "has not yet received a licence from the province of Quebec". That is reported at page 5880 of Hansard. The car rental concession contracts have been in effect since November 1, 1976 but in the case of Host at these airports no revenue has been coming in. To go back to this fiasco of the ministry's handling of car rental concessions at international airports, we note that included in the tender package which the departmental officials gave the applicants at the time tenders were called there was a section dealing with terms and conditions which included, under "Licences, permits, etc." the following:
The lessee shall procure and maintain at the cost and expense of the lessee such licences, permits or approvals from federal, provincial, municipal or other government authorities and such private permits as may be necessary to enable the lessee to furnish the services and to conduct the operations provided for in this agreement.
The car rental concession operators at the departments airports in Quebec must by law obtain a licence from the Quebec government in order to operate their cars outside the confines of the airports. I am informed that Host Rent-a-Car applied to the Quebec transport board for a licence in January of 1977. It is interesting to note that Host was awarded the tender in October, 1976. On June 6, I am told, there will be a hearing or a roll-call at which a date will be decided upon to hear Host's application. It has been challenged by several existing operators at the Quebec airports on the basis that the entry of Host into this limited market will increase competition unduly.
Several questions arise as a result of this particular contract. First, why did Host apply so late for the Quebec licence? Assuming the Host contract was signed and is to be valid for three years, one must ask whether the department's legal branch was aware that paragraph 13 of the agreement which I quoted earlier was not complied with. One might ask whether the legal branch was aware of all the activities in this area undertaken by the department's marketing branch.
Assuming the contract was not signed, which one would doubt, one must ask what is happening in the present situation. We know that Host, which is ranked third at all airports where it won the tender, came in first place in the domestic category
and in third place in the overall ranking. The three divisions are open, domestic and local. It now sits empty at these airports in Quebec. Tilden, which is now in fourth place, sits beside an empty counter and it is no secret than Tilden covets third place at the Quebec airports. Since the minister announced the details of the new airport car rental policy on June 13 the situation has been a total fiasco. It is certainly indicative of the incompetent and shabby manner in which the government has dealt with other issues. It has certainly not handled this policy in a competent way.
A number of questions have been raised in the House by supporters of the government as to the manner in which these particular contracts are awarded and administered. There was an appeal from the Committee for an Independent Canada, for example.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the seven minutes I have available to me-

subtopic: ATOMIC ENERGY OF CANADA LIMITED-STATEMENT CONCERNING ESTABLISHMENT OF PLANT TO PRODUCE PLUTONIUM-GOVERNMENT ACTION
