speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: ATOMIC ENERGY OF CANADA LIMITED-STATEMENT CONCERNING ESTABLISHMENT OF PLANT TO PRODUCE PLUTONIUM-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
-I wanted to raise a question this evening with respect to a rather strange difference of opinion, according to reports which we are receiving both in the House and outside the House, which exists between Atomic Energy of Canada, Ltd. and the government of Canada. Today I asked a question of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with respect to statements by senior officials of AECL. Questions were raised by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence) and questions were raised in the course of the press conference which the Prime Minister holds on a weekly basis. The Prime Minister in his answers appears to take the position that no commitment was made with respect to the construction of a plutonium reprocessing plant in Ontario.
I would like to refer to the debate on the question which was raised by my colleague on May 26, 1977, as reported in Hansard at page 5958, which reads:
In view of the previously expressed government policy, expressed by the Prime Minister himself in this House as late as May 17 last, relating to the undesirability of having in Canada or anywhere in the world plutonium reprocessing plants, I ask, why is the government permitting AECL, a Crown corporation, to engage in an expensive study for the building of a $1.5 billion plutonium extraction plant in Ontario?
The Prime Minister in his response indicated, in effect, that the matter was still under consideration; but he was pressed by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham who quoted the Prime Minister as saying on May 12 last:
"Much of our safeguards position centres around the undesirability of having reprocessing plants. President Carter was stating the view we had already stated many times".
That is the Prime Minister's statement quoted by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham. Subsequently he was asked by the same hon. member whether or not the news we hear about the plant are true, and the Prime Minister said he was going to check with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) to determine exactly what was the situation.
Adjournment Debate
At the press conference later in the day the Prime Minister was asked the following question by one of the participants:
You seemed a bit taken aback in the Commons today when you were asked about reprocessing of nuclear wastes in Ontario. Have you now got clarificaton and can you now give a clear statement that there will not be reprocessing of nuclear material and the making of plutonium in Ontario?
The Prime Minister sloughed off that question by simply saying there was misinformation, that the question was not an accurate statement of the facts and that the matter is still under consideration.
After all this has taken place, we have the unusual prospect of senior officials of AECL coming forward at a press conference called by themselves and stating that they think it would be inappropriate to draw plans for a pilot plutonium plant despite government opposition. As quoted at this press conference the officials said:
... this policy was "out of kilter" with the need to extend uranium resources by reclycling spent fuel into plutonium, which could then be used with thorium to generate more power in existing Canadian reactors.
I go along with my colleague, the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham, that there seems to be a distinct contradiction between the position taken by AECL and taken by the government both inside and outside the House.
What I would like the parliamentary secretary to tell us tonight is precisely what is the government's policy with respect to this matter, why is there a contradiction, and what is the responsibility of the minister with respect to the position taken by AECL, a Crown corporation which has been in the news quite a bit recently with respect to unilateral decisionmaking, without cabinet or ministerial consultation.
I need only talk about the question of the payment of agent's fees in foreign countries for the sale of CANDU reactors. So far as I can make out, the cabinet was completely oblivious to what was going on, not considering it to be a type of policy worthy of cabinet consideration. That seems to be the tendency in this government. They think that by virtue of the delegation of responsibilities to Crown corporations in important policy areas they are somehow absolved of any responsibility on matters of great importance to present and future generations of Canadians.
In my view this is an untenable position for the government to take. If they are not on top of the issues, they are simply being derelict in their duties. I think the parliamentary secretary has the responsibility to tell us whether these officials in the Crown corporations consult the government on policy decisions or whether this government simply allows them to make our nuclear policy without any responsibility or accountability. We know what the examples have been when the AECL has come before the Standing Committee on Public Accounts to answer questions regarding what has happened in their foreign transactions involving CANDU reactors. They have not co-operated as they should have in a committee of the House. I think the parliamentary secretary should give us some explanation of what the relationship is between the minister and officials of AECL with respect to policy in this important area.

May 30, 1977
Adjournment Debate

speakeroldname: Mr. Maurice Dupras (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: ATOMIC ENERGY OF CANADA LIMITED-STATEMENT CONCERNING ESTABLISHMENT OF PLANT TO PRODUCE PLUTONIUM-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is exactly what I will attempt to do. I will attempt to give my hon. colleague an answer which I hope will satisfy him.
AECL held a background briefing for the press on May 27 for the purpose of releasing a document commenting on the brief presented earlier that day by the Coalition for Nuclear Responsibility to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie). At the AECL briefing questions were asked regarding news reports of the February 28 AECL seminar for federal government officials. To clarify the position, the following facts were made clear to the reporters present.
The "once through" cycle in today's CANDU reactors uses natural uranium which is not a weapons usable material. When the fuel is taken out of the reactor, it contains plutonium which is a weapons usable material, but this is widely dispersed throughout the spent fuel, and in the dilute form it presents no risk of diversion and is in any event so radioactive that theft is impossible.
It has always been recognized that uranium supplies are limited and that, if full use of the fission process is to be made, other cycles than "once through" must be employed. Most of the countries with advanced nuclear programs therefore have embarked on programs to extract the plutonium from used fuel and re-use it in a fast reactor; for example, one which burns plutonium and at the same time generates more plutonium which can be extracted and made into more fuel. The United States has now deferred further work on the commercial development of this system on the ground that the existence of weapons usable material in quantity and in numerous places could lead to misuse for weapons purposes.
Canada has no need ever to develop a plutonium fuelled fast breeder reactor, as the CANDU reactor in its present cycle	I
makes more efficient use of uranium than the other types of	I
reactors in use and also has the ability to utilize a thorium	|
cycle with a near breeder capability. Thorium is even more abundant than uranium in the earth's crust. It cannot be used directly for fuel as uranium is, but it can be made into a fuel by putting it into a reactor along with a few per cent of enriched uranium or plutonium which then energizes the thorium to make it a nuclear fuel.
There is a misconception that the U.S. government has withdrawn all support for fuel cycle development. At his press conference of April 7, 1977, President Carter laid down the following policy:
We will continue research and development, but shift away from plutonium, defer dependence on the breeder reactor for commercial use.
We will direct funding of U.S. nuclear research and development programs to accelerate our research into alternative nuclear fuel cycles which do not involve direct access to materials that can be used for nuclear weapons.
One such cycle which is attracting the attention of the U.S. is the CANDU thorium cycle. We expect to be working closely with the U.S. to examine ways of exploiting the benefits of this new resource, thorium, while minimizing the potential for diversion of weapons usable material.
I hope I have reassured the hon. member on the use of plutonium and thorium.
